docs.title: Bank Risk Management Simulation
docs.text:
Put a bank's balance sheet through rising or falling interest rates and watch, day by day, what happens to its books, its regulatory capital and its unrealised losses. Use any US bank, from its public Call Report, or a bank you describe yourself.

The Stress Lab runs on your own computer and opens in your web browser. It is developed by Dr. Mingze Gao at Macquarie Business School for teaching and research.

docs.title: Get started in three steps
docs.text:
1. Install it. Follow Install on your computer: two commands, for Windows, macOS or Linux.
  2. Start it. Run brms in a terminal. The lab opens in your browser.
  3. Try it. The quick start walks you through your first run in five minutes.

docs.title: Learn from real banks
docs.text:
• Why SVB failed

    Run Silicon Valley Bank through the rates of 2022 and see $15bn of losses build up while its capital ratio still looked healthy.

  • The Basel shocks

    Apply the six standard rate shocks to SVB, Signature, First Republic and JPMorgan, and compare which bank is most exposed.

  • SVB's last week

    Add a deposit run and a forced sale of securities, and see what the bank would have realised.

  • Any US bank

    Import a bank from its Call Report by its FDIC number and put it through any scenario.

Prefer code? The lab is also a Python library: see Python and the command line.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: The terms used across these pages, in plain words. Throughout the site, abbreviations with a dotted underline show their meaning when you hover over them.

docs.title: The balance sheet and accounting
docs.text: Amortised cost What a security or loan is carried at when it is not marked to market: the price paid, moved gradually towards the amount repaid at maturity. Changes in market rates do not change it. Fair value What a security would sell for today. When rates rise, the fair value of a fixed-rate bond falls. Unrealised gain or loss Fair value less amortised cost: what the bank would gain or lose if it sold the security today. It becomes realised only when the security is sold. Held to maturity (HTM) Securities the bank intends to keep until they mature. Carried at amortised cost, so their unrealised losses do not appear in the accounts or in capital. Most of SVB's losses were here. Available for sale (AFS) Securities the bank may sell. Carried at fair value; unrealised gains and losses go to equity, in AOCI, rather than to profit. Accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) The part of equity that holds unrealised gains and losses on AFS securities. FVOCI and FVTPL The IFRS 9 names for how a security is measured: at fair value through other comprehensive income (like AFS), or at fair value through profit or loss (a trading book). Net interest income (NII) Interest earned on assets less interest paid on deposits and borrowing: a bank's main source of profit.

docs.title: Capital
docs.text: Regulatory capital The equity a bank must hold to absorb losses, measured as regulators define it. Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) The highest-quality capital: common equity less intangible assets such as goodwill. Under the US "AOCI filter", which smaller US banks could opt into, unrealised losses on AFS securities are left out of CET1; under Basel III they count. Tier 1 and total capital Tier 1 adds Additional Tier 1 (AT1) instruments, such as preferred stock, to CET1. Total capital adds Tier 2 capital, such as subordinated debt. Risk-weighted assets (RWA) The bank's exposures, each weighted by its riskiness: a Treasury bond weighs 0%, a corporate loan around 100%. The lab uses the Basel III standardised approach. Capital ratio Capital divided by RWA. The CET1 ratio must stay above 4.5%, plus buffers. Leverage ratio Tier 1 capital divided by total exposure, with no risk weights.

docs.title: Interest-rate risk
docs.text: Basis point (bp) One hundredth of a percentage point: +200bp means rates rise by 2 percentage points. Yield curve The interest rate for each maturity, from one month to thirty years. The lab uses US Treasury constant maturity (CMT) yields. Interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB) The risk that rate changes reduce a bank's value or income from the loans, securities and deposits it holds, rather than from trading. Economic value of equity (EVE) The present value of the bank's assets less that of its liabilities. ΔEVE is how much it changes under a rate shock. The six Basel shocks Standard rate scenarios from the Basel IRRBB standard: parallel up and down, steepener, flattener, and short rates up and down. See Scenarios. Duration How much a position's value changes when rates move: a duration of 5 years means it loses about 5% for each 1 percentage point rise in rates. Deposit beta The share of a rise in market rates that a bank passes on to depositors. A beta of 0.35 means a +100bp rise lifts the deposit rate by 35bp. Core deposits The stable part of a bank's non-maturity deposits, which in practice stays for years even though customers could withdraw it at any time.

docs.title: Data and the lab
docs.text: Call Report The quarterly financial report every US bank files with its regulators, published by the FDIC. The lab can build a bank from one. See Call Report mapping. Bank file A JSON file listing a bank's positions on a date, from which the lab builds a bank. See Bank file. Scenario The path of interest rates a run follows: actual historical rates or a shock. See Scenarios. Run One bank through one scenario, day by day, with its statements, capital and risk recorded for each day.

docs.title: Basel III Framework
docs.text: Basel III is an internationally agreed-upon regulatory framework developed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) to strengthen the resilience of banks and the financial system. It builds upon previous Basel accords by introducing stricter capital requirements, enhanced risk management practices, and liquidity standards to mitigate systemic risks and financial crises.

docs.title: Basel III in the Stress Lab
docs.text:
The Stress Lab computes a bank's regulatory capital every day of a run: CET1, Tier 1 and total capital, risk-weighted assets under the standardised approach, the capital ratios and the leverage ratio, and the Basel interest-rate shocks to its economic value of equity. It makes some simplifying assumptions, listed in Assumptions; the Metrics page defines each figure.

These pages explain the parts of Basel III behind those figures.

docs.title: Key Components of Basel III
docs.text:
The Basel III framework consists of several key components that ensure banks maintain adequate capital and liquidity buffers to withstand economic stress. These include:

  • Risk-Based Capital Requirements: Ensuring banks hold sufficient capital relative to their risk exposure, primarily through Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA).
  • Definition of Capital: Refining the quality and composition of regulatory capital, emphasizing Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1).
  • Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA): Standardizing how banks measure risk across credit, market, and operational exposures.
  • Leverage Ratio: Setting a minimum leverage ratio to limit excessive borrowing and ensure balance sheet stability.
  • Liquidity Standards: Introducing the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) to enhance short-term and long-term liquidity resilience.

docs.title: Stress Lab
docs.text:
The Stress Lab runs a bank's balance sheet through interest-rate scenarios, one day at a time, with full double-entry accounting. For every day it reports:

  • the books: balance sheet, income statement and every journal entry;
  • regulatory capital: CET1, Tier 1 and total capital ratios, risk-weighted assets, the leverage ratio;
  • unrealised gains and losses: on held-to-maturity (HTM) and available-for-sale (AFS) securities and on loans;
  • interest-rate risk in the banking book: economic value of equity (EVE) under the six Basel shocks, duration and net interest income (NII) sensitivity.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
• Supervisors and central bankers. Take any US bank's Call Report and see how its capital and unrealised losses respond to the Basel shocks, or to the rate path you are worried about.
  • Researchers. Script thousands of runs from Python and get tidy pandas data back.
  • Students and teachers. Watch the accounting of a bank day by day, and see why SVB failed while its regulatory capital looked fine.

docs.title: What it answers
docs.text:
• How much of a bank's equity would unrealised losses wipe out if rates rose by 200bp?
  • What would its CET1 ratio be if unrealised losses on AFS securities counted, as they do under Basel III?
  • Which of these banks is most exposed to a steepening of the yield curve?
  • If the bank sold its AFS book to meet a deposit run, what would it realise, and would the cash be enough?

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The lab runs on your own computer and opens in your browser; nothing is uploaded.

uv tool install "brms[web]>=0.2"   # or: python -m pip install "brms[web]>=0.2" (Python 3.11+)
brms

Step by step for Windows, macOS and Linux, and what to do if something goes wrong: Install on your computer. pip install brms alone installs the Python library and the command line without the browser app.

docs.title: The banks it ships with
docs.text:
Bank As of Why it is interesting Silicon Valley Bank end-2021 $125bn of long, fixed-rate securities funded by deposits that left; failed March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank end-2022 Ten weeks before it failed, with $15bn of unrealised losses on HTM securities Signature Bank end-2021 Failed two days after SVB First Republic Bank end-2021 Long fixed-rate mortgages; failed May 2023 JPMorgan Chase Bank end-2021 The largest US bank, for comparison Five teaching examples Jan 2022 One instrument each (a Treasury, a mortgage, a floating loan…) and a small diversified bank

The real banks are built from their public Call Reports (FDIC BankFind) and saved with the package, so they work offline. See how a Call Report becomes a bank.

docs.title: How good is it?
docs.text: On Silicon Valley Bank, the engine reproduces the unrealised losses SVB reported for 2022 to within a few percentage points of amortised cost. Validation has the details and the gaps.

docs.title: Install on your computer
docs.text:
The Stress Lab runs entirely on your own computer. You install it once, start it from a terminal, and use it in your web browser at http://127.0.0.1:8765. Nothing is uploaded: your banks and runs stay in a folder on your computer. Only two things use the internet: installing, and importing a bank's Call Report from the FDIC.

It works on Windows, macOS and Linux. A run needs about 200 MB of memory and one processor core.

docs.title: The easy way: with uv
docs.text:
uv is a small installer for Python programs. It downloads a suitable version of Python for the lab, so you do not need to install Python yourself, and it keeps the lab separate from anything else on your computer.

1. Open a terminal.

  • Windows: press Win, type PowerShell and open Windows PowerShell.
  • macOS: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal and open it.
  • Linux: open your terminal application.

2. Install uv. Copy the line for your system, paste it into the terminal and press Enter.

WindowsmacOS and Linux 
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Then close the terminal and open a new one, so that it finds the uv command.

3. Install the lab.

uv tool install "brms[web]>=0.2"

This takes a minute the first time.

4. Start it.

brms

The terminal shows:

BRMS Stress Lab running at http://127.0.0.1:8765/
Your banks and runs are saved in C:\Users\you\.brms-web
Keep this window open while you use the lab. To stop it, click Quit in the lab or press Ctrl+C here.

and your browser opens the lab. If it does not, open http://127.0.0.1:8765 yourself. The lab opens in a second or two. The first time after installing, the demo banks take up to half a minute to prepare: they show preparing and fill in as each one is ready.

Now follow the quick start.

Just trying it?

uvx --from "brms[web]>=0.2" brms starts the lab without installing it.

docs.title: With pip
docs.text:
If you already use Python 3.11 or later, install the lab into a virtual environment:

WindowsmacOS and Linux 
py -3.12 -m venv brms-env
brms-env\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install "brms[web]>=0.2"
brms

python3 -m venv brms-env
source brms-env/bin/activate
python -m pip install "brms[web]>=0.2"
brms

Activate the environment again (the second line) each time you open a new terminal.

pip install brms, without [web], installs the Python library and the command line only.

docs.title: Every day
docs.text:
To Do this start the lab open a terminal and run brms stop it click Quit at the top right of the lab, or press Ctrl+C in its terminal open it again in the browser run brms again: if the lab is already running, it opens the browser at it update to the latest version uv tool upgrade brms (with pip: python -m pip install -U "brms[web]") uninstall uv tool uninstall brms, then delete the data folder if you no longer need it

Closing the browser tab does not stop the lab. Stopping it stops any run still in progress (the run is marked failed; start it again later). Your banks and finished runs are kept.

docs.title: Your data
docs.text:
Banks you import and runs you make are saved in a folder in your home directory: C:\Users\<you>\.brms-web on Windows, ~/.brms-web on macOS and Linux. They are still there the next time you start the lab. To keep them somewhere else, start the lab with brms --data-dir <folder>, or set the environment variable BRMS_WEB_HOME.

Each run takes a few MB. Delete runs you no longer need on the Runs page. The demo banks come with the lab and cannot be deleted.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
brms [--port 8765] [--data-dir FOLDER] [--workers N] [--no-browser]
Option Meaning --port the port in the address (default 8765) --data-dir where banks and runs are saved (default $BRMS_WEB_HOME or ~/.brms-web) --workers how many runs execute at the same time (default: one per processor core, leaving one free, at most four) --no-browser do not open the browser

The lab listens only to your own computer (127.0.0.1): other computers on your network cannot reach it.

The browser app talks to the lab through a JSON API, documented at http://127.0.0.1:8765/docs while the lab is running.

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text:
brms or uv: command not found. Close the terminal and open a new one. If it still fails after installing uv, run uv tool update-shell, then open a new terminal.

"Port 8765 is used by another program". Start the lab on another port, brms --port 8800, and open http://127.0.0.1:8800.

The browser shows an old page after an update. Reload the page (Ctrl+Shift+R, or Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac).

pip says Python is too old, or installs version 0.1. The lab needs Python 3.11 or later. Use the uv method above, which brings its own Python.

Importing a Call Report fails behind a company proxy. The import downloads the filing from api.fdic.gov. Set the proxy before starting the lab, for example set HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:8080 (Windows) or export HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:8080 (macOS and Linux). Or download the filing on another machine with python -m brms.lab call-report --cert N --date D --out bank.json and import the bank file instead.

A run fails. The run's page shows the error. Runs never change the bank, so you can start another one. If the lab itself stops, start it again: runs that were in progress are marked failed.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Five minutes, no code. You will run Silicon Valley Bank through the actual interest rates of 2022 and see what happened to its securities and its capital.

docs.title: 1. Install and start
docs.text:
The lab runs on your own computer. If you have not installed it yet, follow Install on your computer (about five minutes). Then, in a terminal:

brms

Your browser opens at http://127.0.0.1:8765. If it does not, open that address yourself. Keep the terminal open while you use the lab. To stop it, click Quit at the top right of the lab, or press Ctrl+C in the terminal.

Port already in use?

Start it on another port: brms --port 8800.

docs.title: 2. Pick a bank
docs.text:
The Banks page lists the banks that ship with the lab: five real banks (case studies) and five small teaching examples.

Click Silicon Valley Bank, end-2021.

docs.title: 3. Look at the balance sheet
docs.text:
• The tiles at the top give the size of the bank, its equity, its annual operating costs and whether the AOCI filter is on (see below).
  • Balance sheet at start is the bank on 31 December 2021, built from its Call Report. Figures in tables are in USD thousands, as filed: 208,724,118 is $208.7bn.
  • Positions lists every security and loan with its carrying value, fair value and unrealised gain or loss. Click a column heading to sort.

docs.title: 4. Run a scenario
docs.text:
In Run a scenario on the right:

  1. Leave Scenario on Historical rates (the US Treasury yields that actually happened).
  2. Leave Horizon at 12 months.
  3. Click Run scenario.

The run takes about fifteen seconds; the page shows its progress and then the results.

docs.title: 5. Read the results
docs.text:
The tiles summarise the year:

Tile What it says for SVB in 2022 CET1 ratio, end 19.2%: regulatory capital looked strong… HTM unrealised −$12.7bn: …but its held-to-maturity securities had lost $12.7bn of value AFS unrealised −$3.4bn more on available-for-sale securities Net income +$2.2bn of profit after costs and tax

Against equity of $14.9bn, the unrealised losses were larger than all of the bank's capital, yet the CET1 ratio rose. Why? HTM securities are held at amortised cost, so their losses never reach the books, and SVB used the AOCI filter, which keeps AFS losses out of CET1 too.

The charts below the tiles show each measure day by day: the rate path, capital ratios, unrealised gains and losses by book, the balance sheet, economic value, duration, NII sensitivity and more. Hover over a chart to read values.

docs.title: 6. Look inside the books
docs.text:
Scroll down to Books. Drag the slider, or click on any chart, to pick a day:

  • Statements shows the balance sheet that day and the income statement since the start.
  • Journal shows every journal entry posted that day, with the instrument it belongs to.
  • Positions at end lists each position's carrying value, amortised cost and fair value.

docs.title: 7. Stress it
docs.text:
Go back to the bank (click its name at the top) and click Run all Basel shocks. The lab starts seven runs (historical rates plus the six standardised interest-rate shocks of the Basel framework) and opens a comparison when they finish:

The summary table is sorted by the lowest CET1 ratio each scenario reached.
