docs.text:
• Tutorial: SVB through 2022 explains these numbers and shows what happens when unrealised losses count in capital.
  • Tutorial: the Basel shocks compares four banks under the same shock.
  • Tutorial: SVB's last week adds a deposit run and a fire sale.
  • Tutorial: a bank from its Call Report loads any US bank.

docs.title: Validation: Silicon Valley Bank, 2022
docs.text: Does the lab reproduce the unrealised losses a real bank reported? We take Silicon Valley Bank's balance sheet at the end of 2021, run it through the actual Treasury yields of 2022, and compare its unrealised losses at the end of 2022, as a share of amortised cost, with what SVB reported. Rates of loss, not amounts, are compared, because SVB bought, sold and was repaid securities during 2022 while the lab holds the end-2021 book.

docs.title: Capital at the start
docs.text:
Each case study's capital on its first market day in the lab, against the same bank's Call Report (USD billions):

Bank Equity, filed Equity, lab RWA, filed RWA, lab CET1 ratio, filed CET1 ratio, lab Silicon Valley Bank, end-2021 14.8 14.6 98 93 14.9% 15.7% Silicon Valley Bank, end-2022 15.5 15.6 111 103 15.3% 17.2% Signature Bank, end-2021 7.8 7.8 77 74 9.6% 9.9% First Republic Bank, end-2021 15.9 15.9 125 104 9.7% 11.6% JPMorgan Chase Bank, end-2021 302.8 301.6 1,582 1,684 16.9% 15.2%
  • Equity matches to within 1.5%. The small gaps are the first day's marks and two days of income.
  • RWA differ because the lab applies the Basel III standardised approach (CRE20). US banks report under the US capital rules, which weight residential mortgages at 50%; Basel III weights low loan-to-value mortgages at 20–40%. So the lab's RWA are lower for mortgage-heavy banks (First Republic) and its CET1 ratios higher. JPMorgan reports under the advanced approaches, with lower RWA than the standardised approach gives.
  • CET1 excludes preferred stock (Additional Tier 1) and intangibles, as the filing does.

The browser app shows this comparison for any Call Report bank, on its page under Filing and lab.

docs.title: From the Call Report alone
docs.text:
The case study bank, built from SVB's Call Report with no other input. The comparison is with the bank's end-2022 Call Report.

Case HTM, lab HTM, reported AFS, lab AFS, reported Call Report only −14.0% −16.6% −13.6% −8.9% With the 10-K's AFS mix −14.1% −16.6% −13.2% −8.9%
  • HTM is within 2.6 percentage points.
  • AFS losses are overstated. The filing does not say which securities are AFS. With the proportional split, the AFS book takes the bank's overall maturity profile, including long municipal bonds and 25-year MBS pools, while SVB's AFS Treasuries were mostly 1–5 years. Giving the class mix alone does not fix this: the maturity, not the class, is missing. SVB also turned over a third of its AFS book in 2022, which no static book reproduces.

Reproduce: python -m brms.lab.examples.svb_call_report.

docs.title: From the 10-K
docs.text:
A hand-built bank from SVB Financial Group's 10-K (USD millions): each securities book is one instrument sized to the portfolio duration SVB reported.

Case HTM, lab HTM, reported AFS, lab AFS, reported Bullet bonds, durations as at end-2021 (HTM 4.1, AFS 3.5 years) −9.7% −16.6% −8.1% −8.9% Bullet bonds, durations as at end-2022 (HTM 6.2, AFS 3.6 years) −13.3% −16.6% −8.3% −8.9% HTM as an agency MBS pool (1.64% coupon, 25 years remaining) −16.7% −16.6% −8.1% −8.9%
  • AFS (mostly Treasuries) is reproduced to within one percentage point when its duration is right.
  • HTM as a bullet bond is understated: a bullet bond cannot lengthen as SVB's MBS did (from 4.1 to 6.2 years) when prepayments slowed.
  • HTM as an MBS pool lands on the reported rate. Most of the improvement comes from treating the book as a long amortising pool. The pool's projected prepayment speed falls from 9.5% to 6.2% a year and its duration rises from 6.6 to 6.8 years. The remaining term is an assumption: 20 years gives −15.1%, 28 years −17.5%.

Reproduce: python -m brms.lab.examples.svb.

docs.title: What this tells you
docs.text:
• The lab's valuation of fixed-rate securities through a real rate path is accurate when it is given the right maturity profile.
  • From a Call Report alone, total unrealised losses are close and HTM is within a few points. The HTM/AFS split by maturity is the main uncertainty. Use the 10-K, or the FR Y-9C, when you need the AFS figure precisely.
  • Both checks are part of the test suite (tests/lab/test_svb.py, tests/lab/test_svb_call_report.py).

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: What the lab does, and does not do, to a bank as time passes. Read this before drawing conclusions from a run.

docs.title: The balance sheet is static
docs.text:
The lab holds the bank's book as it was on the as-of date. It does not grow, originate new loans, take new deposits or buy securities. As time passes:

  • loans amortise and mature; the cash comes back and stays as cash;
  • bonds pay coupons and mature into cash, unless reinvestment is on, which rolls each maturing bond into a new par bond of the same term at the market rate;
  • deposits stay unless you give them run-off or withdrawals.

Cash earns nothing. A bank with a lot of maturing assets therefore loses interest income over a long horizon: set reinvestment on when you want a constant-size balance sheet.

docs.title: Securities
docs.text:
• HTM (AMORTIZED_COST): carried at amortised cost by the effective interest method. Fair value is computed every market day but never enters the books.
  • AFS (FVOCI): carried at fair value; the gap to amortised cost sits in accumulated OCI (AOCI) in equity. Interest income is at the effective rate. Selling recycles the AOCI into profit.
  • Trading (FVTPL): carried at fair value; every mark goes to profit.
  • Fair value discounts each position's cash flows on the day's Treasury curve plus a constant credit spread, calibrated so that the position is worth its reported fair value on the as-of date. Spreads do not change in a run: the lab isolates interest-rate risk.
  • Mortgage-backed securities prepay faster when mortgage rates fall below the pool's note rate. Fair value and EVE project prepayments at the speed today's rates imply. Realised paydowns use a constant speed fixed on the as-of date.

docs.title: Loans
docs.text: Loans are held at amortised cost, on the books at par. Fixed-rate loans amortise on schedule; floating-rate loans pay Prime plus a spread, resetting monthly. Loans get a fair value (for unrealised gains and losses and EVE) from the same constant credit spread. Credit losses and provisions are not modelled.

docs.title: Deposits
docs.text:
• Rate. Each deposit pays its rate on the as-of date plus beta times the change in the 3-month Treasury yield since then, never below zero. Interest accrues daily and is paid on the first of each month.
  • Balance. runoff_rate removes a share of the balance continuously over the year, and withdrawals remove a fraction on given dates. The cash leaves with them. A run's liquidity stress (browser: Liquidity stress; Python: DepositStress) adds run-off from the start date and a one-off withdrawal to every deposit not marked as a borrowing.
  • Core deposits in EVE. Following the Basel standard (SRP31), part of a non-maturity deposit can be treated as stable: its core_share runs off in equal monthly amounts over twice its core_maturity (its average life), and EVE discounts that run-off on the curve. The rest reprices overnight. When rates rise, the core deposits are worth less as a liability, which offsets part of the loss on fixed-rate assets. Without a core share, a deposit reprices overnight and offsets nothing.
  • Call Report banks get the Basel caps, weighted by how much of their deposits is insured: insured deposits count as retail (90% core with a 5-year average life for noninterest-bearing, transactional deposits; 70% and 4.5 years for interest-bearing), uninsured deposits as wholesale (50%, 4 years). A bank funded by uninsured deposits, like SVB (95% uninsured), therefore has less stable funding than one funded by insured retail deposits. These are the regulatory caps, so the lab's ΔEVE is on the generous side for the bank. Untick Core deposits on import (or pass core_deposits=False) to treat every deposit as repricing overnight.
  • In NII sensitivity, a deposit reprices by its beta: a +200bp shock raises its cost by beta × 200bp over the part of the year left. Noninterest-bearing deposits (beta 0) do not reprice.

docs.title: Profit, tax and dividends
docs.text:
• Interest (accruals, coupons, premium and discount amortisation), marks on trading positions and realised gains and losses on sales are computed position by position.
  • Non-interest expense and income (operating) are annual amounts booked through cash at 1/365 a day. Without them, the bank has no costs.
  • Income tax is accrued so that the tax for the period is the rate times the period's pre-tax profit, never below zero. A loss after profits reverses tax already booked. No deferred tax asset is recognised for losses beyond that.
  • Dividends pay out the payout ratio times the period's profit after tax. Dividends paid are never taken back after a later loss.

docs.title: Capital
docs.text:
• CET1 = total equity − intangible assets − preferred stock in equity − (AOCI, when the AOCI filter is on).
  • Tier 1 = CET1 + preferred stock in equity + other additional Tier 1; total capital = Tier 1 + Tier 2. Call Report banks take preferred stock and Tier 2 from the filing.
  • Credit RWA uses the Basel III standardised approach (CRE20), not the US capital rules, so a US bank's RWA in the lab differ from its filing (see Validation): each security and loan is weighted by its issuer type and rating (sovereign, public-sector entity, bank, corporate), mortgages by loan-to-value, retail loans at 75%. Cash is 0%; other assets 100%; intangibles are deducted.
  • Operational RWA is an input; for Call Report banks the lab estimates it with the Basel standardised approach (details).
  • Market-risk RWA is not modelled: trading positions are weighted as credit exposures.
  • The leverage ratio is Tier 1 over total assets less intangibles (on-balance-sheet exposure).

docs.title: Not modelled
docs.text: Credit losses and provisions; liquidity ratios (LCR, NSFR); hedges and derivatives; changes in credit spreads; deposit and loan growth; management actions. A negative cash balance is the lab's signal that the bank needs funding. The lab does not borrow on the bank's behalf.

docs.title: Reading a run
docs.text: What every part of a run's page shows, and how to read it.

docs.title: The header
docs.text: The scenario, any liquidity stress, the horizon and the options used (reinvestment, AOCI filter). Download CSV gives every daily metric, the daily statements, every position's daily values, or the journal. Run another goes back to the bank.

docs.title: The tiles
docs.text:
Tile Meaning CET1 ratio, end Common Equity Tier 1 capital over risk-weighted assets on the last day, with the change since the start CET1 ratio, low The lowest CET1 ratio of the run, and the day it happened: the stress point Total capital ratio Total capital over RWA, with the Tier 1 ratio below Leverage ratio Tier 1 capital over total exposure (assets less intangibles) Worst ΔEVE / Tier 1 Change in the economic value of equity under the worst of the six Basel shocks, over Tier 1 capital, on the last day. Supervisors flag banks below −15% Net income Profit after costs and tax over the run HTM unrealised / AFS unrealised Fair value less amortised cost of held-to-maturity and available-for-sale securities on the last day

Money is in dollars, scaled (K, M, B, T). Green is a gain, red a loss.

docs.title: The charts
docs.text:
Every chart covers the run day by day. Hover for exact values; click to choose the day shown in Books (an amber line marks it on every chart).

Chart What to look for Treasury yields The scenario: the 3-month, 2-year and 10-year yields Capital ratios CET1, total capital (hidden when equal to CET1) and leverage ratios Unrealised gains and losses By book: HTM securities, AFS securities, loans. These move against the 10-year yield Assets The balance sheet's assets, stacked: watch cash grow as loans and bonds run off Worst ΔEVE / Tier 1 Interest-rate exposure of the whole banking book, every day Asset duration Effective duration of the bond and loan book in years: how far its value moves for a 1% rate change NII sensitivity, 12 months Change in the next year's net interest income if rates move ±200bp, from the repricing gap Net interest margin Interest income less interest expense over interest-earning assets, trailing year, annualised (needs 30 days) Cash and funding Cash against funding (deposits and borrowings): with a liquidity stress, cash below zero is the funding the bank would need

docs.title: Books
docs.text:
The Books panel shows the bank's accounts on any day of the run:

  • Statements: the balance sheet that day, and the income statement from the start of the run to that day.
  • Journal: every double-entry journal entry posted that day: accruals, coupons, marks, paydowns, operating costs, tax. Each entry names the instrument it belongs to. Type in the filter box to search by account or description.
  • Positions at end: each security and loan with its carrying value, amortised cost, fair value and unrealised gain or loss on the last day it was held.

Tables show amounts as filed: Call Report banks in USD thousands (the panel says so).

docs.title: Comparing runs
docs.text: Compare overlays runs on the same charts: CET1 ratio, total unrealised gains and losses, worst ΔEVE / Tier 1, net interest margin and the 10-year yield. The summary table is sorted by each run's lowest CET1 ratio. Runs of different banks are labelled with the bank's name, and their unrealised gains and losses are shown as a percentage of each bank's equity at the start, so banks of different sizes compare.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Why does the CET1 ratio rise while the bank loses billions in value? HTM losses never reach the books, and with the AOCI filter AFS losses do not reach CET1. Meanwhile profits add to capital. Run with the AOCI filter off to see AFS losses in capital, and look at the unrealised gains and losses chart for what the books do not show.

Why is ΔEVE so large? Long fixed-rate assets lose value when rates rise, and only the stable (core) part of deposits offsets that. A bank funded by uninsured or rate-sensitive deposits has little core funding. See assumptions.

Why do some positions disappear? They matured or were sold. Positions at end shows them as Closed with their last values.

Why is cash negative? Deposits left (run-off or withdrawals) faster than assets turned into cash. The lab shows the funding gap; it does not borrow.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: A scenario is the path of interest rates the bank lives through: the US Treasury curve (constant maturity yields, from 1 month to 30 years) and the Prime rate, for every business day from the start date to the end of the horizon. Everything before the start date is real history, so curves and floating-rate fixings up to the start are the actual ones.

docs.title: Historical rates
docs.text: The rates that actually happened, from the data shipped with the package (US Treasury yields and the Prime rate, daily from 1990 to the end of 2025). The horizon cannot go past the end of the data: the app tells you the longest horizon available for a bank.

docs.title: The six Basel shocks
docs.text:
Shock Shift at maturity t years (basis points) Parallel up +200 Parallel down −200 Short rates up +300 × e−t/4 Short rates down −300 × e−t/4 Steepener −0.65 × 300 e−t/4 + 0.9 × 150 (1 − e−t/4) Flattener +0.8 × 300 e−t/4 − 0.6 × 150 (1 − e−t/4)

These are the US-dollar shock sizes of the Basel standard on interest-rate risk in the banking book (SRP31). At the short end the steepener moves rates by −195bp and the flattener by +240bp; at the long end by +135bp and −90bp.

docs.title: Parallel and key-rate shifts
docs.text:
• Parallel shift: any number of basis points at every maturity (parallel+150, parallel-50 on the command line).
  • Key-rate shift: basis points at chosen maturities. Between them the shift is linear in maturity; beyond the first and last it is flat. In the browser app the maturities are 3M, 1Y, 2Y, 5Y, 10Y and 30Y; in Python any (years, bp) points:
from brms.lab import KeyRateShift, Shock
Shock(KeyRateShift(((0.25, 300), (2, 200), (10, 50), (30, 25))), label="bear flattener")

docs.title: How a shock is applied
docs.text:
• The shift is added to each Treasury yield by maturity (1M, 3M, 6M, 1Y, 2Y, … 30Y) on the start date, then the curve stays at that level for the rest of the horizon. A shock is a jump to a new, constant curve, not a path.
  • Phase-in (ramp_days): the shift grows linearly from zero on the start date to its full size after that many days, then stays.
  • Prime moves by the shock's shift at 3 months, so floating-rate loans reprice with short rates.
  • Floor (Python: Shock(..., floor=0.0)): shocked yields below the floor are set to it. By default yields may go negative.
  • The shift applies to par yields (the quoted yields), which is close to, but not exactly, a shift of zero rates.

docs.title: Which scenario to use
docs.text: Question Scenario What did actually happen to this bank? Historical rates Is the bank an IRRBB outlier? How does it compare with peers? The six Basel shocks (Run all Basel shocks) What if rates rise gradually over a year? Parallel up with a 365-day phase-in What if the curve inverts? Key-rate shift: up at the short end, down at the long end A supervisory or central-bank scenario Key-rate shift with the scenario's curve move

docs.title: Bank file reference
docs.text: A bank file is a JSON object describing a bank's balance sheet on one date. Build it with python -m brms.lab build-bank bank.json --out bank.zip, the browser app's Import page, or brms.lab.bank_file.build_bank. A complete example: riverside.json.

docs.title: Top level
docs.text:
Key Required Meaning name no the bank's name as_of yes balance-sheet date, YYYY-MM-DD (a business day); the simulation starts the next day cash yes cash and balances at banks deposits no list of deposits (and other funding) positions no list of positions: securities and loans other_assets no assets not modelled one by one (premises, other); carried unchanged, risk-weighted 100% intangible_assets no goodwill and other intangibles; carried unchanged, deducted from CET1 other_liabilities no liabilities not modelled one by one; carried unchanged operating no operating flows: costs, fees, tax, dividends regulatory no regulatory inputs unit no the currency amount one unit of the file stands for (1000 if amounts are in thousands); used by the browser app for display story, source, reported no free text and metadata, shown by the browser app; ignored by the engine

Equity is not given: it is cash + positions + other and intangible assets − deposits − other liabilities. It must be positive.

docs.title: Deposits
docs.text:
Key Required Meaning id yes unique id; the position is pos-<id> name no display name balance yes balance on the as-of date interest_rate yes annual rate on the as-of date (0.01 = 1%) beta no share of each change in the reference yield passed on (default 0) reference_tenor no the Treasury yield the rate follows (default "3 Mo") runoff_rate no continuous annual run-off (0.1 = 10% a year) withdrawals no [["YYYY-MM-DD", fraction], …]: a fraction of the balance then outstanding leaves on that date core_share no share of the balance that is stable for interest-rate risk (Basel SRP31); default 0 borrowing no true for wholesale borrowings carried as a funding line (FHLB advances, repos): a run's deposit stress leaves them alone core_maturity with core_share average life of the core balance in years (Basel caps: 5 retail transactional, 4.5 retail other, 4 wholesale)

Use a deposit with beta: 1.0 for floating-rate borrowings.

docs.title: Positions
docs.text:
Every position has these keys, plus the instrument terms of its type:

Key Required Meaning id yes unique id; the position is pos-<id> type yes instrument type (below) name no display name (generated from the terms otherwise) issuer yes* {"name": …, "issuer_type": …, "credit_rating": …} credit_rating no an issue rating, which takes precedence over the issuer's basis no AMORTIZED_COST (default), FVOCI or FVTPL book no BANKING (default) or TRADING amortized_cost for AMORTIZED_COST, FVOCI clean amortised cost on the as-of date fair_value for FVOCI, FVTPL clean fair value on the as-of date; optional at amortised cost

* Mortgages are weighted by ltv instead and need no issuer for the risk weight, but every position should name one.

Values are clean: without accrued interest, which the lab computes from the terms. The position is treated as bought at the close of the as-of date at its book value; its credit spread is calibrated to fair_value (or to the book value when no fair value is given).

issuer_type: SOVEREIGN, PSE (public-sector entities: agencies, states, municipalities), MDB, BANK, CORPORATE, SME, SECURITIES_FIRM, FINANCIAL_INSTITUTION, INSURANCE_COMPANY, INDIVIDUAL.

credit_rating: AAA, AA_PLUS, AA, AA_MINUS, A_PLUS, A, A_MINUS, BBB_PLUS, BBB, BBB_MINUS, BB_PLUS, BB, BB_MINUS, B_PLUS, B, B_MINUS, CCC_PLUS, CCC, CCC_MINUS, CC, C, D, UNRATED.

docs.title: Instrument types
docs.text: Dates are YYYY-MM-DD; periods are a number and a unit, "30Y", "6M", "1M"; rates are decimals.

docs.title: Bonds: fixed_rate_bond, treasury_note, treasury_bond
docs.text: Key Meaning face_value face (par) amount coupon_rate annual coupon rate issue_date, maturity_date dates frequency coupon frequency, "6M" (default, semi-annual) or "1Y", "3M"

docs.title: Loans: amortizing_fixed_rate_loan, residential_mortgage, commercial_mortgage
docs.text:
Key Meaning face_value principal interest_rate annual rate issue_date start of the loan (the as-of date for a loan described as of today) maturity term from issue_date, e.g. "30Y" frequency payment frequency (mortgages default monthly; other loans semi-annual: give "1M") ltv loan-to-value at origination (mortgages; required for the risk weight)

Level payments (principal plus interest) amortise the loan to zero at maturity. Loans must be on the books at par: amortized_cost equal to the principal outstanding.

docs.title: variable_rate_loan
docs.text: Key Meaning face_value, issue_date, maturity as above spread margin over Prime (0.015 = 1.5%) benchmark_family "prime" repricing_frequency, payment_frequency e.g. "1M" principal_repayment_mode "bullet" (all at maturity) or "sinking" (equal instalments) floor_rate, cap_rate optional floor and cap on the all-in rate

docs.title: mortgage_backed_security
docs.text:
An agency mortgage pass-through.

Key Meaning face_value pool balance coupon_rate pass-through rate paid to holders issue_date the as-of date maturity remaining term, e.g. "25Y" wac the mortgages' note rate (default coupon + 0.5%) pricing_cpr the constant annual prepayment rate for realised paydowns (default: the model's rate on the as-of date) prepayment the prepayment model (all optional): turnover_cpr (0.06), max_cpr (0.50), refi_center (0.0075), refi_width (0.0075), mortgage_spread (0.017)

The annual prepayment rate is an S-curve in the refinancing incentive, wac − mortgage rate, where the mortgage rate is the 10-year Treasury zero rate plus mortgage_spread. It rises from turnover_cpr towards max_cpr, reaching the midpoint at an incentive of refi_center. Pools must be on the books at par and held at AMORTIZED_COST or FVOCI.

docs.title: Operating
docs.text:
All optional; annual amounts in the file's unit.

Key Meaning noninterest_expense salaries, premises, technology and other costs per year noninterest_income fees and other non-interest income per year tax_rate income tax as a share of pre-tax profit (0.21 = 21%) dividend_payout share of profit after tax paid as dividends (0.3 = 30%)

docs.title: Regulatory
docs.text: Key Meaning aoci_filter true to exclude accumulated OCI from CET1 (US option for banks below the largest size) operational_rwa operational-risk RWA, added to credit RWA additional_tier1 Additional Tier 1 capital instruments tier2 Tier 2 capital preferred_equity preferred stock included in equity that counts as Additional Tier 1: excluded from CET1, added back in Tier 1

docs.title: Building
docs.text: The builder checks the file and stops with a message that names the position at fault. See Tutorial: build a bank from scratch for the common messages.

docs.title: Call Report mapping
docs.text: How brms.lab.call_report turns a bank's Call Report into a bank file. Items come from the FDIC BankFind financial data (FDIC field names in code), in USD thousands, as filed. Income items are year-to-date and are annualised (×4 for March, ×2 for June, ×4/3 for September).

docs.title: Date
docs.text: The bank is described as of the report date, or the Friday before when the quarter ends on a weekend (the last business day). The official report date is kept in source.report_date.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
Call Report Becomes Cash and due from banks CHBAL + fed funds sold and reverse repos FREPO cash Non-mortgage debt securities by remaining maturity or repricing (RC-B Memo 2: SCNM3LES, SCNM3T12, SCNM1T3, SCNM3T5, SCNM5T15, SCNMOV15) fixed-rate bullet bonds maturing at the bucket midpoint (1.5 months, 7.5 months, 2, 4, 10 and 20 years), split into Treasuries (share SCUST, sovereign AA+) and other issuers (agencies and municipalities, PSE AA+) Mortgage pass-throughs by remaining maturity (SCPT…) agency MBS pools with that remaining term (2 months, 8 months, 2, 4, 10 and 25 years) Other mortgage-backed securities by expected average life (SCO3YLES, SCOOV3Y) bullet bonds at 2 and 6 years Loans repricing or maturing within 3 months (LNRS3LES, LNOT3LES) Prime floaters: monthly reset, 3-year bullet, spread = loan yield − Prime Other 1–4 family loans by remaining maturity (LNRS…) residential mortgages at the bucket midpoint, ltv as given (default 0.8) Other loans by remaining maturity (LNOT…) amortising fixed-rate loans at the bucket midpoint, corporate unrated Intangible assets INTAN intangible_assets (deducted from CET1) Total assets ASSET less everything above other_assets (risk-weighted 100%)

Loans are scaled so that they sum to net loans LNLSNET.

Securities yield and book. Every security pays the bank's securities yield: securities income ISC (annualised) over the five-quarter average of securities SC5. Loans pay the loan yield: loan income ILNLS over average loans LNLSGR5.

The Memorandum 2 buckets combine HTM at amortised cost and AFS at fair value. Each class is split between HTM and AFS in the bank's overall proportion (SCHA : SCAF), unless an AFS mix is given (afs= in Python: fair value by class treasury, other_debt, pass_through, other_mbs). HTM pieces get fair value in the ratio SCHF / SCHA; AFS pieces get amortised cost in the ratio SCAA / SCAF. So the HTM and AFS totals and their fair values match the filing.

docs.title: Funding
docs.text:
Call Report Becomes Noninterest-bearing deposits DEPNIDOM a deposit at 0% Interest-bearing deposits DEP − DEPNIDOM a deposit at the bank's deposit cost (EDEP annualised over the balance), passing through deposit_beta (default 0.35) of moves in the 3-month yield Other borrowed money OTHBRF + fed funds purchased and repos FREPP + subordinated notes SUBND one floating-rate liability (beta 1) at its cost, (EINTEXP − EDEP) annualised over the balance Total liabilities LIAB less the above other_liabilities

Core deposits. With core_deposits on (the default), each deposit line gets a core_share and core_maturity from the Basel SRP31 caps, weighted by the uninsured share of domestic deposits DEPUNINS / DEPDOM (all uninsured when the filing does not give it). Insured deposits count as retail: 90% core with a 5-year average life for noninterest-bearing (transactional) deposits, 70% and 4.5 years for interest-bearing. Uninsured deposits count as wholesale: 50% and 4 years. Borrowings get no core share.

docs.title: Income
docs.text:
Call Report Becomes Total noninterest expense NONIX operating.noninterest_expense Total noninterest income NONII operating.noninterest_income Applicable income taxes ITAX / income before taxes IBEFTAX operating.tax_rate (21% if pre-tax income is not positive or the rate is outside 0–50%) Cash dividends EQCDIV / net income NETINC operating.dividend_payout, capped at 100% (0 without a profit)

Credit-loss provisions are not used: the lab does not model credit losses.

docs.title: Capital
docs.text:
• regulatory.aoci_filter: an input (default on).
  • regulatory.preferred_equity: perpetual preferred stock EQPP (Additional Tier 1, part of equity).
  • regulatory.tier2: Tier 2 capital as reported, RBCT2.
  • regulatory.operational_rwa: estimated with the Basel III standardised approach for operational risk. The business indicator is the smaller of |net interest income| and 2.25% of earning assets (ERNAST), plus non-interest income. It is multiplied by 12% up to $1bn, 15% from $1bn to $30bn and 18% above, with the internal loss multiplier at 1. RWA is 12.5 times the result.

docs.title: Kept for comparison
docs.text: reported holds the filing's total assets ASSET, equity EQ, CET1 capital RBCT1C, CET1 ratio RBCT1CER, RWA RWAJ, HTM and AFS amortised cost and fair value, intangibles and trading assets. Equity in the lab should be within about 1% of EQ.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The filing does not say which securities are HTM and which AFS, or their maturities by book. With the proportional split, AFS takes the bank's overall maturity profile, which overstates AFS losses for banks whose AFS books are short (see Validation).
  • Trading assets, equity securities and derivatives are in other_assets, at constant value.
  • Deposits have no run-off; add it in the bank file.

docs.title: How the engine works
docs.text: The lab is a daily accounting simulation. Each calendar day it values every position, generates the day's transactions from them, posts those as double-entry journal entries, and computes the day's metrics. Everything you see is read from the ledger and the valuations, never estimated on the side.

docs.title: One day
docs.text:
1. Market data. On business days the Treasury curve is built from the scenario's yields (a smooth zero curve through the quoted par yields), and Prime fixings are updated.
  2. Valuation. For every open position:
    • accrued interest since the last payment;
    • amortised cost (effective-interest method for bonds; principal outstanding for loans and pass-throughs);
    • fair value on market days: the position's remaining cash flows (projected, for floating loans and MBS) discounted on the curve plus its credit spread, less accrued interest;
    • carrying value: amortised cost or fair value, depending on the accounting basis.
  3. Transactions. Rules turn valuations and contracts into transactions:
    • interest accruals and their settlement;
    • premium and discount amortisation;
    • mark-to-market of AFS and trading positions;
    • coupon and principal payments, maturities and scheduled sales;
    • deposit interest, run-off and withdrawals;
    • operating costs, fees, income tax and dividends.
  4. Posting. Each transaction becomes journal entries in a chart of accounts organised under IFRS 9 categories (amortised cost, FVOCI, FVTPL). Every entry balances.
  5. Metrics. On market days: capital, RWA, ratios, profitability and interest-rate risk.

The books reconcile every day. Each account holding positions equals the sum of its positions' carrying values, and assets equal liabilities plus equity. The test suite checks this for every day of every shipped bank.

docs.title: Starting a bank
docs.text:
A simulation file (.zip) holds the instruments, positions, the opening balances of every account, and market data. Building one from a bank file:

  1. creates each instrument from its terms;
  2. books each position as bought at the close of the as-of date at its book value (plus accrued interest), and books deposits, other assets and liabilities, with equity as the balance;
  3. solves each bond's effective interest rate from its amortised cost and calibrates its credit spread to its fair value;
  4. closes the books, so the run's income statement starts from zero.

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text: Bond and loan cash flows, curves and pricing use QuantLib. Results are pandas data frames. Runs are deterministic: the same bank and scenario give the same numbers.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Static balance sheet: no new business; maturing assets become cash (or roll over, with reinvestment).
  • No credit risk dynamics: no defaults, provisions or spread changes.
  • Simple deposit behaviour: rates follow a constant beta, balances a constant run-off or scheduled withdrawals, and the core share in EVE is fixed (the Basel caps for Call Report banks).
  • No liquidity metrics (LCR, NSFR), derivatives or hedge accounting.
  • US focus: Treasury curve, Prime rate, US calendars; Basel standardised approaches.
  • Mortgage-backed securities pay down at a fixed speed; only their value responds to rates.

See Assumptions for the details that matter when reading results.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: Computed on every market day and returned in RunResult.metrics (Python), metrics.csv (command line) and Download CSV → Metrics, daily (browser). Money is in the bank's unit; ratios are fractions (0.12 = 12%).

docs.title: Balance sheet
docs.text: Column Definition TOTAL_ASSETS total assets of the balance sheet (as if the books were closed that day) TOTAL_LIABILITIES total liabilities TOTAL_EQUITY total equity EQUITY_TO_ASSETS total equity / total assets INTEREST_EARNING_ASSETS carrying value of open securities and loans

docs.title: Capital
docs.text: Column Definition CET1_CAPITAL total equity − intangible assets − preferred stock in equity − accumulated OCI (only when the AOCI filter is on) TIER1_CAPITAL CET1 + preferred stock in equity + other additional Tier 1 (inputs) TOTAL_CAPITAL Tier 1 + Tier 2 (input) CREDIT_RWA standardised credit risk-weighted assets: exposures (carrying value plus accrued interest) × CRE20 risk weights; other assets 100%, cash 0% OPERATIONAL_RWA operational-risk RWA (input, or estimated for Call Report banks) TOTAL_RWA credit + operational RWA CET1_RATIO, TIER1_RATIO, TOTAL_CAPITAL_RATIO capital / total RWA LEVERAGE_RATIO Tier 1 / (total assets − intangible assets)

docs.title: Profitability
docs.text:
Over the trailing year (or since the start, when shorter), annualised; empty for the first 30 days.

Column Definition NET_INTEREST_MARGIN (interest income − interest expense) / average interest-earning assets ROA net income / average total assets ROE net income / average total equity

docs.title: Interest-rate risk in the banking book
docs.text:
Column Definition EVE economic value of equity: present value of banking-book securities and loans on the day's curve (each with its credit spread), plus cash, less the present value of core deposits' run-off, less the other deposits and interest payable at book value DELTA_EVE_WORST the most negative change in EVE across the six Basel shocks, revaluing every cash flow on the shocked curve (MBS re-project their prepayments) DELTA_EVE_WORST_TO_TIER1 DELTA_EVE_WORST / Tier 1; supervisors flag below −15% ASSET_DURATION effective duration of the securities and loans: the change in their value for a ±1bp parallel shift, per unit of value, in years NII_SENSITIVITY_UP, NII_SENSITIVITY_DOWN change in the next 12 months' net interest income for a +200bp / −200bp parallel shift, from the repricing gap: each item reprices at its next reset or maturity, weighted by the time left in the year

In EVE, the core part of each deposit is the discounted run-off of its core balance; the rest reprices overnight. In NII sensitivity, deposits reprice by their beta (see assumptions).

docs.title: Positions
docs.text:
RunResult.carrying_value, .fair_value and .amortized_cost hold one column per position:

Value Meaning carrying value what the account holds: amortised cost (HTM, loans) or fair value (AFS, trading) amortised cost cost rolled forward at the effective interest rate (bonds) or less principal repaid (loans, MBS); not kept for trading positions fair value clean present value of the remaining cash flows on the day's curve plus the position's spread; market days only

Unrealised gain or loss = fair value − amortised cost.

docs.title: Tutorial: build a bank from scratch
docs.text:
Time: 30 minutes · You need: a text editor, and the browser app or the command line · You will learn: how to describe a balance sheet in a bank file, build it and run it.

A bank file is a JSON document listing a bank's positions on one date (the as-of date), with their contract terms and book values. The lab turns it into a simulation: every security and loan is treated as bought on the as-of date at its book value, and equity is whatever balances the books.

We will build Riverside Community Bank, a $1.6bn bank with Treasuries, agency MBS, municipal bonds, mortgages, business loans and consumer loans. The finished file is riverside.json.

docs.title: Step 1: the frame
docs.text:
{
  "name": "Riverside Community Bank",
  "as_of": "2021-12-31",
  "cash": 60000000,
  "deposits": [],
  "positions": []
}
  • as_of is the balance-sheet date. The simulation starts the next day. Pick a business day.
  • Amounts are in currency units (here dollars). Use the same unit everywhere. If you work in thousands, add "unit": 1000 so the browser app shows dollars.
  • cash is cash and balances at other banks.

docs.title: Step 2: deposits
docs.text:
"deposits": [
  {"id": "checking", "name": "Checking accounts", "balance": 680000000, "interest_rate": 0.0, "runoff_rate": 0.05,
   "core_share": 0.9, "core_maturity": 5},
  {"id": "savings", "name": "Savings and money market", "balance": 520000000, "interest_rate": 0.001, "beta": 0.3,
   "core_share": 0.7, "core_maturity": 4.5},
  {"id": "time", "name": "Time deposits", "balance": 230000000, "interest_rate": 0.008, "beta": 0.6}
]
Field Meaning balance balance on the as-of date interest_rate rate paid on the as-of date (0.001 = 0.1%) beta share of each move in the 3-month Treasury yield passed on (0.3 = 30%); the rate never goes below zero runoff_rate share of the balance that leaves per year, continuously (0.05 = 5% a year) withdrawals one-off outflows: [["2023-03-09", 0.25]] takes 25% of the balance on 9 March 2023 core_share, core_maturity for interest-rate risk: the share of the balance that is stable, and its average life in years. Here the Basel caps for retail checking (90%, 5 years) and savings (70%, 4.5 years); the time deposits get none

Interest is accrued daily and paid on the first of each month.

docs.title: Step 3: securities
docs.text:
Each position has an id, a type, its contract terms, an issuer, an accounting basis and its book values:

{"id": "ust", "type": "treasury_note", "face_value": 150000000, "coupon_rate": 0.0125,
 "issue_date": "2021-11-30", "maturity_date": "2026-11-30",
 "issuer": {"name": "US Treasury", "issuer_type": "SOVEREIGN", "credit_rating": "AA_PLUS"},
 "basis": "FVOCI", "amortized_cost": 149500000, "fair_value": 149000000}
  • basis is the accounting category: AMORTIZED_COST (held to maturity), FVOCI (available for sale) or FVTPL (trading).
  • amortized_cost and fair_value are clean values (without accrued interest). FVOCI needs both; AMORTIZED_COST needs amortized_cost (and fair_value if you have it); FVTPL needs fair_value.
  • The lab solves each bond's effective interest rate from its amortised cost, and calibrates a credit spread so that its fair value on the as-of date is the one you gave.
  • issuer drives the credit risk weight: SOVEREIGN, PSE (agencies, municipalities), BANK, CORPORATE, INDIVIDUAL… with a credit_rating such as AA_PLUS.

An agency mortgage pass-through and a municipal bond:

{"id": "mbs", "type": "mortgage_backed_security", "face_value": 250000000, "coupon_rate": 0.02,
 "issue_date": "2021-12-31", "maturity": "28Y",
 "issuer": {"name": "Agency MBS", "issuer_type": "PSE", "credit_rating": "AA_PLUS"},
 "basis": "AMORTIZED_COST", "amortized_cost": 250000000, "fair_value": 248000000},
{"id": "muni", "type": "fixed_rate_bond", "face_value": 60000000, "coupon_rate": 0.025,
 "issue_date": "2020-06-01", "maturity_date": "2035-06-01",
 "issuer": {"name": "State and municipal", "issuer_type": "PSE", "credit_rating": "AA"},
 "basis": "AMORTIZED_COST", "amortized_cost": 61000000, "fair_value": 62000000}

The MBS pool's prepayments speed up when mortgage rates fall and slow when they rise; see the bank file reference.

docs.title: Step 4: loans
docs.text:
Loans are held at amortised cost and must be on the books at par (amortised cost = face value outstanding):

{"id": "mortgages", "type": "residential_mortgage", "face_value": 500000000, "interest_rate": 0.031,
 "issue_date": "2021-12-31", "maturity": "30Y", "ltv": 0.7,
 "issuer": {"name": "Households", "issuer_type": "INDIVIDUAL"},
 "basis": "AMORTIZED_COST", "amortized_cost": 500000000},
{"id": "business", "type": "variable_rate_loan", "face_value": 400000000, "spread": 0.015,
 "issue_date": "2021-12-31", "maturity": "5Y", "benchmark_family": "prime",
 "repricing_frequency": "1M", "payment_frequency": "1M", "principal_repayment_mode": "bullet",
 "issuer": {"name": "Local businesses", "issuer_type": "CORPORATE"},
 "basis": "AMORTIZED_COST", "amortized_cost": 400000000},
{"id": "consumer", "type": "amortizing_fixed_rate_loan", "face_value": 120000000, "interest_rate": 0.045,
 "issue_date": "2021-12-31", "maturity": "5Y", "frequency": "1M",
 "issuer": {"name": "Consumers", "issuer_type": "INDIVIDUAL"},
 "basis": "AMORTIZED_COST", "amortized_cost": 120000000}
  • A mortgage needs ltv (loan-to-value, 0.7 = 70%) for its risk weight.
  • The business loan pays the Prime rate plus 1.5%, resetting monthly.
  • Periods are written "30Y", "5Y", "1M".

docs.title: Step 5: everything else
docs.text:
"other_assets": 30000000,
"other_liabilities": 15000000,
"operating": {"noninterest_expense": 28000000, "noninterest_income": 6000000, "tax_rate": 0.21, "dividend_payout": 0.3},
"regulatory": {"aoci_filter": true, "operational_rwa": 60000000}
  • other_assets (premises, goodwill, other) and other_liabilities are carried unchanged. Other assets are risk-weighted at 100%.
  • operating gives the annual non-interest expense (salaries, premises, technology) and income (fees), the tax rate, and the share of profit after tax paid out as dividends. Without it, the bank has no costs and pays no tax.
  • regulatory: whether AOCI is excluded from CET1, and the operational-risk RWA (the lab does not derive it from a bank file). additional_tier1 and tier2 can also be given.

docs.title: Step 6: build and run it
docs.text:
BrowserCommand line
  1. Start brms and open Import.
  2. Drop riverside.json on From a bank file (or paste it), then click Build from bank file.
  3. On the bank's page, click Run all Basel shocks.
python -m brms.lab build-bank riverside.json --out riverside.zip
python -m brms.lab run riverside.zip --scenario historical --scenario parallel+200 \
    --scenario steepener --months 12 --out results

results/historical/, results/parallel_up/ and results/steepener/ then hold metrics.csv (every metric, every market day), carrying_value.csv, fair_value.csv and summary.json.

Output of the command line:

scenario            CET1 end  CET1 min   dEVE/T1     net income
historical            18.01%    15.89%   -70.42%     18,091,207
parallel_up           18.13%    15.88%   -44.70%     19,417,565
steepener             17.73%    15.89%   -52.28%     15,047,752

Riverside starts with a CET1 ratio of 15.9% and builds capital through the year. Its economic value is still very exposed: 30-year mortgages and 28-year MBS funded by deposits, of which only the core part offsets the loss. The worst ΔEVE (−70%) is on the first day of the historical run, at the low rates of January 2022, when long fixed-rate assets are most sensitive. Under the +200bp shock the bank starts from higher rates, so the same Basel shocks cost less (−45%). By the end of 2022 both runs are at about −35%. See assumptions.

docs.title: When something is wrong
docs.text:
The builder checks the file and stops with a message naming the position:

Message Fix Position 'x' (FVOCI) needs 'fair_value' Add the missing value. loans bought at a premium or discount are not supported yet Make the loan's amortized_cost equal its face_value. The bank file implies non-positive equity Assets must exceed deposits and other liabilities. cannot be risk-weighted: the mortgage has no loan-to-value ratio Add ltv to mortgages. Unknown prepayment model fields / Unknown operating fields Check the spelling against the reference.

docs.title: Tutorial: the Basel shocks
docs.text: Time: 20 minutes · You need: the browser app · You will learn: what the six Basel interest-rate shocks are, how to run them, and how to compare banks under the same shock.

docs.title: The six shocks
docs.text:
The Basel Committee's standard for interest-rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB, SRP31) defines six shocks to the yield curve. For US dollars:

Shock What moves Size Parallel up every maturity +200bp Parallel down every maturity −200bp Short rates up short maturities, fading with maturity +300bp at the short end Short rates down the same, downwards −300bp at the short end Steepener short rates down, long rates up −195bp short, +135bp long Flattener short rates up, long rates down +240bp short, −90bp long

The short-rate shocks decay with maturity t in years as e−t/4. The steepener and flattener combine the short and long shapes. Supervisors use these shocks to compare banks: a bank whose economic value falls by more than 15% of Tier 1 capital in the worst of the six is an outlier that draws attention.

In the lab a shock is applied on the start date to the Treasury curve, and the curve then stays at that shocked level for the whole horizon. You can also phase a shock in over a number of days.

docs.title: Part 1: all six shocks on one bank
docs.text:
1. Open Banks → Silicon Valley Bank, end-2021.
  2. Leave the horizon at 12 months and click Run all Basel shocks.

The lab starts seven runs (historical rates plus the six shocks) and opens Compare when they finish. The summary table is sorted by each run's lowest CET1 ratio. Look at:

  • HTM unrealised: the parallel-up shock costs SVB −$10.3bn on HTM securities, and the actual path of 2022 cost −$12.7bn. The real 2022 was worse than the regulatory +200bp shock, because the 10-year yield rose about 240bp.
  • Worst ΔEVE/T1: SVB's economic value falls by more than half of its Tier 1 capital in the worst shock. That makes it a clear outlier against the 15% threshold.

docs.title: Part 2: four banks under the same shock
docs.text:
Now compare four banks under Parallel up (+200bp), with unrealised AFS losses counted in capital, as Basel III requires.

For each of Silicon Valley Bank, end-2021, Signature Bank, end-2021, First Republic Bank, end-2021 and JPMorgan Chase Bank, end-2021:

  1. Open the bank.
  2. In Run a scenario, choose Basel IRRBB shocks → Parallel up (+200bp), horizon 12, AOCI filter: Off.
  3. Click Run scenario.

Then open Runs, tick the four runs and click Compare 4 selected. Each run is labelled with its bank. Because the banks differ in size, the comparison shows unrealised gains and losses as a share of each bank's equity at the start: SVB's are almost twice its equity, at about −180%.

Bank Lowest CET1 ratio Worst ΔEVE / Tier 1 HTM unrealised AFS unrealised Signature Bank 7.4% −20% −$0.4bn −$1.5bn First Republic Bank 11.0% −42% −$3.4bn −$0.7bn Silicon Valley Bank 12.2% −55% −$10.3bn −$2.8bn JPMorgan Chase Bank 13.6% −10% −$28.4bn −$23.3bn

How to read it:

  • Capital. With AOCI counted, the shock hits CET1 on day one through AFS losses. Signature starts with the thinnest capital and drops to 7.4%. All four then recover as profits accumulate.
  • Economic value. ΔEVE revalues every asset and liability at the shocked rates, including the stable (core) part of deposits. Three of the four banks are outliers against the 15% threshold; JPMorgan is not. SVB is the most exposed: long securities, funded by deposits that were 95% uninsured and so count as less stable. First Republic's exposure is in long fixed-rate mortgages, which are loans rather than securities: they show up in EVE and in loan unrealised losses, not in HTM or AFS.
  • Size. JPMorgan's dollar losses are the largest, but against its capital its economic-value loss is the smallest, and its larger share of insured retail deposits offsets more of it. Its $46bn of goodwill and other intangibles is deducted from CET1, as First Republic's and Signature's preferred stock is (it counts as Additional Tier 1, not common equity).

Deposits in ΔEVE

Core deposits follow the Basel caps, weighted by each bank's insured share (assumptions). Untick Core deposits when importing a bank to see the exposure of the assets alone.

docs.title: Part 3: phase a shock in
docs.text: A shock that arrives over a year is gentler than one that arrives overnight, because the bank keeps earning while it builds. On SVB, run Parallel up (+200bp) with Phase in over (days) set to 365, and compare it with the instant shock. The unrealised losses end in the same place; the CET1 path is smoother.

docs.title: Part 4: your own curve shift
docs.text: Choose Key-rate shift… and enter a shift in basis points at 3M, 1Y, 2Y, 5Y, 10Y and 30Y. Between those maturities the shift is interpolated linearly; beyond them it is flat. For example, a bear flattener: 3M +300, 1Y +250, 2Y +200, 5Y +100, 10Y +50, 30Y +25.

docs.title: What you have learned
docs.text:
• The six Basel shocks give a common yardstick across banks.
  • Capital measures (with or without AOCI) and economic value tell different stories: one is the accounting view, the other the market view of the whole balance sheet.
  • A shock's speed matters for capital, not for the final unrealised loss.

docs.title: Tutorial: a bank from its Call Report
docs.text:
Time: 15 minutes · You need: the browser app and an internet connection · You will learn: how to load any US insured bank, what the lab builds from its filing, and which assumptions to check.

Every FDIC-insured bank in the United States files a Call Report each quarter: its balance sheet, income statement and capital, with securities and loans broken down by how soon they mature or reprice. The FDIC publishes these filings through its free BankFind API, and the lab reads them.

docs.title: Step 1: find the bank's certificate number
docs.text:
Each bank has an FDIC certificate number.

  1. Go to FDIC BankFind.
  2. Search for the bank by name.
  3. The certificate number (FDIC Cert #) is on the bank's page.

Some examples: Silicon Valley Bank 24735, Signature Bank 57053, First Republic Bank 59017, JPMorgan Chase Bank 628, Bank of America 3510, Wells Fargo Bank 3511.

Banks, not holding companies

Call Reports cover the insured bank, not its parent holding company (for example Silicon Valley Bank, not SVB Financial Group). Figures differ somewhat from the group's 10-K.

docs.title: Step 2: import it
docs.text:
In the browser app, open Import. Under From a US Call Report:

  1. FDIC certificate: the number from Step 1.
  2. Quarter end: the filing to use. The filing for a quarter appears about 30 days after quarter end.
  3. Mortgage loan-to-value: the lab needs a loan-to-value ratio to risk-weight 1–4 family mortgages; Call Reports do not give one. 0.8 is a reasonable average.
  4. Deposit beta: the share of each move in the 3-month Treasury yield passed on to interest-bearing deposits. 0.35 is roughly the US average through 2022–23; banks with rate-sensitive depositors are higher.
  5. AOCI filter: tick it for banks that exclude AOCI from capital (most US banks below the largest size); untick it for the largest banks, or to apply Basel III.
  6. Core deposits in EVE: keep it ticked to treat the stable part of deposits as long-lived in the economic-value measure, following the Basel caps weighted by the bank's insured share.
  7. Click Build from Call Report.

The lab fetches the filing, builds the bank (a few seconds) and opens its page.

docs.title: Step 3: check what was built
docs.text:
The lab turns the filing into about 50 positions. Check the bank page against the filing:

  • Total assets and equity should be close to the reported figures. Equity is the balancing figure of what the lab models, plus other assets and liabilities carried as they are.
  • Operating costs / yr shows the annualised non-interest expense, fee income and effective tax rate taken from the income statement.
  • Positions shows the securities and loans. Names tell you what each one is: for example 1.52% 2046/12/31 MBS is the mortgage pass-throughs with more than 15 years to maturity, at the bank's average securities yield.

How each line of the Call Report becomes a position is set out in the Call Report mapping. The points that matter most:

Assumption Why it matters What to do HTM and AFS split in the bank's overall proportion within each security class The filing does not say which securities sit in which book If you know the AFS mix (10-K, FR Y-9C), use the Python afs= option (below) Each maturity bucket becomes one instrument at the bucket midpoint Drives duration and therefore unrealised losses Accept it for comparisons across banks Deposits do not run off A deposit run is the key liquidity risk Add a Liquidity stress to the run, or runoff_rate and withdrawals to the bank file (example) Operational-risk RWA is estimated Affects the capital ratios' level Compare with the reported RWA in the bank file's reported block

docs.title: Step 4: run it
docs.text: Run historical rates or the Basel shocks as in the Quick start. Remember that the bank is frozen at the filing date: the lab does not add new loans, new deposits or securities purchases.

docs.title: From Python or the command line
docs.text:
The same import, without the browser:

Command linePython 
python -m brms.lab call-report --cert 24735 --date 2021-12-31 --out svb.json
python -m brms.lab build-bank svb.json --out svb.zip
python -m brms.lab run svb.zip --scenario historical --scenario parallel+200 --months 12 --out results

import datetime
from pathlib import Path
import json

from brms.lab import Historical, run
from brms.lab.bank_file import build_bank, default_market_frames, prime_on
from brms.lab.call_report import bank_file_from_call_report, fetch_call_report

items = fetch_call_report(24735, "2021-12-31")
frames = default_market_frames()
bank = bank_file_from_call_report(
    items,
    prime=prime_on(frames, datetime.date(2021, 12, 31)),
    deposit_beta=0.35,
    # SVB's AFS book by class, from its 10-K (USD thousands): mostly Treasuries.
    afs={"treasury": 15_850_000, "other_debt": 257_000, "pass_through": 8_589_000, "other_mbs": 2_525_000},
)
Path("svb.json").write_text(json.dumps(bank, indent=1))
result = run(build_bank(Path("svb.json"), frames, Path("svb.zip")), Historical(), months=12)
print(result.summary)

The bank file is plain JSON: open svb.json, edit any assumption (a deposit's beta, a runoff_rate, the operating block), and build again.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Message Meaning The report date must be a quarter end Use 31 March, 30 June, 30 September or 31 December. No Call Report for FDIC certificate … on … The bank did not file for that quarter (not yet published, merged or closed), or the number is wrong. The FDIC API answered 429 The API is busy; the lab retries three times. Wait a minute and try again. Cannot compute … the denominator is 0 The filing lacks an item the mapping needs (a bank with no securities, for example). Build the bank from a bank file instead.

docs.title: Python and the command line
docs.text: Everything the browser app does is available from Python, for notebooks, research and batch runs, and from the command line.

docs.title: Run a scenario
docs.text:
from brms.data import DEFAULT_DATA_FOLDER
from brms.lab import Historical, run

svb = DEFAULT_DATA_FOLDER.parent / "case_svb_2021.zip"   # a shipped case study
result = run(svb, Historical(), months=12)
print(result.summary)

run(simulation, scenario, ...) takes a simulation zip (shipped, or built with build_bank) and:

Argument Meaning months horizon from the start date, e.g. months=12; or give end=datetime.date(...). With neither, the run goes to the end of the simulation's market data regulatory a RegulatoryConfig (brms.core.models.regulatory) overriding the AOCI filter, operational RWA, AT1 and Tier 2; default: the bank's own operating an OperatingConfig (brms.core.models.operating) overriding costs, fees, tax rate and dividend payout; default: the bank's own sales {"pos-afs": date}: sell positions at fair value on market days (AFS and trading positions only); default none reinvest_maturities True rolls each maturing bond into a new par bond of the same term at the market rate; default False (maturities stay in cash) deposit_stress a DepositStress(runoff_rate=…, withdrawal=…, withdrawal_date=…): extra run-off from the start date and/or a one-off withdrawal, applied to every deposit except borrowings sell_afs_on sell every AFS (FVOCI) security on that date, or the next market day

To switch the AOCI filter off while keeping the bank's other settings:

import dataclasses
from brms.core.services import build_core_services

regulatory = dataclasses.replace(build_core_services(simulation_zip=svb).bank.regulatory, aoci_filter=False)
counted = run(svb, Historical(), months=12, regulatory=regulatory)

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
from brms.core.metrics.risk.interest_rate_risk.eve import Scenario
from brms.lab import Historical, KeyRateShift, Shock

Historical()                                   # the stored Treasury yields and Prime rate
Shock(Scenario.PARALLEL_UP)                    # +200bp from the start date
Shock(Scenario.STEEPENER, ramp_days=90)        # phased in over 90 days
Shock(KeyRateShift(((0.25, 300), (2, 200), (10, 50))), label="bear flattener")   # bp by maturity (years)
Shock(Scenario.PARALLEL_DOWN, floor=0.0)       # yields floored at 0%

The six Basel scenarios are PARALLEL_UP, PARALLEL_DOWN, STEEPENER, FLATTENER, SHORT_UP and SHORT_DOWN. See Scenarios for the shapes and how a shock moves the Prime rate.

docs.title: Many scenarios at once
docs.text:
from brms.lab import run_many

results = run_many(svb, [Historical(), Shock(Scenario.PARALLEL_UP), Shock(Scenario.STEEPENER)],
                   months=12, workers=4)

Each scenario runs in its own process, in parallel. Put the call under if __name__ == "__main__": in scripts, as for any Python multiprocessing code.

docs.title: What a run returns
docs.text:
A RunResult holds plain pandas data:

Attribute Contents metrics one row per market day, one column per metric: CET1_RATIO, LEVERAGE_RATIO, DELTA_EVE_WORST_TO_TIER1, ASSET_DURATION, … carrying_value, fair_value, amortized_cost one row per day, one column per position id statements balance sheet and income statement (since the start) per market day, long form: date, section, account, balance journal every journal line: date, entry, kind, description, position, account, debit, credit positions every position: id, instrument, name, type, basis, book, side, status yields the scenario's Treasury curve (percent) balance_sheet, income_statement the statements on the last day, as dictionaries summary headline numbers: CET1 at the end and its low point, worst ΔEVE/Tier 1, net income, and unrealised_end (HTM, AFS and loans on the last market day) unrealised(position_id) fair value less amortised cost on the last day both exist

Fair values exist only on market days (business days with a Treasury curve), while carrying value and amortised cost exist every calendar day. Take the last market day with .dropna(how="all").iloc[-1] when you combine them.

Examples:

result.metrics["CET1_RATIO"].plot()                    # with matplotlib installed

# unrealised gain or loss of every HTM security on the last day
securities = ["FIXED_RATE_BOND", "TREASURY_NOTE", "TREASURY_BOND", "MORTGAGE_BACKED_SECURITY"]
held = result.positions[(result.positions["basis"] == "AMORTIZED_COST") & result.positions["type"].isin(securities)]
gap = (result.fair_value - result.amortized_cost).dropna(how="all")[held["id"]].iloc[-1].dropna()
print(gap.sum(), result.summary["unrealised_end"]["htm"])   # the same total

# the balance sheet on 30 June 2022
import datetime
s = result.statements
s[(s["date"] == datetime.date(2022, 6, 30)) & s["section"].isin(["assets", "liabilities", "equity"])]

# every entry booked for one position
result.journal[result.journal["position"] == "pos-pt-ov15-htm"]

docs.title: Build banks
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from brms.lab.bank_file import build_bank, default_market_frames

simulation = build_bank(Path("riverside.json"), default_market_frames(), Path("riverside.zip"))

default_market_frames() returns the Treasury yields and Prime rate shipped with the package (daily, from 1990 to the end of 2025). To use your own, pass {"yields": df, "benchmarks": df} with the same columns (Treasury CMT tenors such as "3 Mo", "10 Yr", in percent; DPRIME).

From a Call Report: see the Call Report tutorial.

docs.title: The command line
docs.text:
python -m brms.lab call-report --cert 24735 --date 2021-12-31 --out svb.json \
    [--ltv 0.8] [--deposit-beta 0.35] [--no-aoci-filter] [--no-core-deposits]
python -m brms.lab build-bank svb.json --out svb.zip [--yields yields.csv] [--benchmarks prime.csv]
python -m brms.lab run svb.zip --scenario historical --scenario parallel+200 \
    [--months 12] [--workers 4] [--out results] \
    [--deposit-runoff 0.5] [--withdrawal 0.25 --withdrawal-date 2023-03-09] [--sell-afs-on 2023-03-08]

Scenario names for run: historical, parallel+200, parallel-200, steepener, flattener, short+300, short-300, or any parallel shift such as parallel+150 or parallel-50. run prints a summary table and writes, for each scenario, a folder under --out named after the scenario (historical, parallel_up, parallel_down, steepener, flattener, short_up, short_down, parallel+150bp…) holding metrics.csv, carrying_value.csv, fair_value.csv and summary.json. Liquidity stress: --deposit-runoff 0.5, --withdrawal 0.25 --withdrawal-date 2023-03-09 and --sell-afs-on 2023-03-08. Sales of single positions and reinvestment are available from Python.

brms [--port 8765] [--data-dir DIR] [--workers N] [--no-browser] starts the browser app on your computer; see the options.

docs.title: Tutorial: SVB through 2022
docs.text: Time: 15 minutes · You need: the browser app (brms) · You will learn: how unrealised losses build up when rates rise, why they did not show in SVB's regulatory capital, and what changes when they count.

docs.title: The story
docs.text:
At the end of 2021 Silicon Valley Bank had $209bn of assets. Deposits had poured in during 2021 and SVB had invested most of them in long-dated, fixed-rate securities: Treasuries and agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS) yielding about 1.5%. In 2022 the Federal Reserve raised rates from near zero to over 4%. Fixed-rate securities lose value when rates rise. In March 2023 depositors ran, SVB sold securities at a loss to pay them, and it failed within two days.

You will now replay 2022 on SVB's actual end-2021 balance sheet.

docs.title: Step 1: open the bank
docs.text:
Start the app (brms), click Banks, then Silicon Valley Bank, end-2021.

Note three numbers on the tiles:

  • Total assets $208.7bn.
  • Equity $14.9bn: everything the shareholders can lose before depositors lose.
  • AOCI filter: On. Keep this in mind for Step 4.

Scroll to Positions and sort by Carrying value. The biggest holdings after the floating loans are MBS pools (1.52% 2046/12/31 MBS) and bonds (1.52% 2028/1/1 Fixed Rate Bond), held at Amortised cost (held to maturity, HTM) or FVOCI (available for sale, AFS).

HTM and AFS

A held-to-maturity security is carried at amortised cost: its price changes never reach the balance sheet. An available-for-sale security (FVOCI under IFRS 9) is carried at fair value, and its price changes go to accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI), a part of equity, not to profit.

docs.title: Step 2: run 2022
docs.text: In Run a scenario: Historical rates, 12 months, AOCI filter: As the bank (on). Click Run scenario.

docs.title: Step 3: read what happened
docs.text:
Measure 1 Jan 2022 30 Dec 2022 10-year Treasury yield 1.5% 3.9% HTM unrealised loss about −$1bn −$12.7bn (worst: −$14.7bn on 20 Oct) AFS unrealised loss about −$0.1bn −$3.4bn Net income for the year +$2.2bn CET1 ratio 15.7% 19.2%

Look at the Unrealised gains and losses chart: the HTM line falls with every rise in the 10-year yield on the Treasury yields chart.

By October the losses on securities alone (about −$18bn) were larger than SVB's entire equity ($14.9bn). If SVB had had to sell everything, it would have been insolvent. Yet its CET1 ratio rose, from 15.7% to 19.2%, because:

  1. HTM losses are not in the books at all (amortised cost);
  2. AFS losses are in AOCI, but the AOCI filter removes AOCI from CET1, an option US banks below the largest size could take;
  3. the bank kept earning: $2.2bn of profit after costs and tax adds to capital.

Open Books and drag the slider to 20 October 2022. In Statements, Accumulated OCI shows the AFS loss inside equity. The HTM loss appears nowhere on the balance sheet.

docs.title: Step 4: count the AFS losses in capital
docs.text:
Under the full Basel III standard, AOCI counts in CET1. Go back to the bank, and in Run a scenario set:

  • AOCI filter: Off
  • Label: Historical, AOCI counted

Run it. Now:

AOCI filter on AOCI counted CET1 ratio at start 15.7% 15.4% Lowest CET1 ratio 15.7% (on day 1) 13.7% (14 Jun 2022) CET1 ratio at end 19.2% 15.3%

With AOCI counted, capital falls through the first half of 2022 as AFS losses mount, then recovers slowly as profits accumulate. Even then, the much larger HTM loss is still invisible.

docs.title: Step 5: compare the two runs
docs.text: Open Runs, tick both runs and click Compare 2 selected. The CET1 ratio chart shows the two paths side by side; the summary table gives their lowest points.

docs.title: What you have learned
docs.text:
• Rising rates cut the value of fixed-rate securities. For SVB, the 2022 losses on securities were larger than all its equity.
  • Accounting choices (HTM, AFS with the AOCI filter) kept those losses out of regulatory capital, so the CET1 ratio gave no warning.
  • The losses become real only when securities are sold, which is what a deposit run forces. SVB's last week plays that out.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Run the Parallel up (+200bp) shock instead of historical rates. How does a sudden 200bp move compare with the gradual rise of 2022?
  • Open Silicon Valley Bank, end-2022 and run 3 months of historical rates. This is the bank the market was looking at in early 2023.
  • Read the Basel shocks tutorial to compare SVB with other banks.

Why the lab's numbers differ from SVB's own

The lab holds the end-2021 balance sheet fixed: it does not replay SVB's 2022 purchases, sales or deposit outflows, and it rebuilds the securities from the Call Report's maturity buckets. SVB reported HTM unrealised losses of $15.2bn (−16.6% of amortised cost) at the end of 2022; the lab gets −$12.7bn (−13%). See Validation.

docs.title: Tutorial: SVB's last week
docs.text: Time: 20 minutes · You need: the browser app, or Python 3.11+ with pip install brms · You will learn: how to add a deposit run and a sale of securities to a scenario, and how to read a liquidity gap from the books.

docs.title: The story
docs.text:
On Wednesday 8 March 2023 SVB announced it had sold $21bn of available-for-sale (AFS) securities at a $1.8bn loss and needed to raise capital. On Thursday 9 March depositors withdrew $42bn, about a quarter of all deposits. On Friday the bank was closed.

You will replay that week on SVB's balance sheet at the end of 2022, twice: once holding everything, once selling the AFS book on 8 March. Both times a quarter of deposits leaves on 9 March.

docs.title: In the browser
docs.text:
1. Open Banks → Silicon Valley Bank, end-2022.
  2. In Run a scenario: Historical rates, horizon 3 months.
  3. Open Liquidity stress (optional) and set:
    • Withdrawal (% of deposits): 25, on 2023-03-09.
  4. Label: Run, hold. Click Run scenario.
  5. Back on the bank, run it again with the same withdrawal and also Sell all AFS securities on 2023-03-08. Label: Run, sell AFS.
  6. In Runs, tick both and click Compare 2 selected. Then open each run, drag the Books slider to 7, 8 and 9 March 2023, and read Cash and Cash Equivalents, Accumulated OCI and Net income in Statements.

The withdrawal applies to deposits only; SVB's other borrowings stay.

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
The same two runs, on the case study shipped with the package:

import datetime

from brms.data import DEFAULT_DATA_FOLDER
from brms.lab import DepositStress, Historical, run

svb = DEFAULT_DATA_FOLDER.parent / "case_svb_2022.zip"
run_on_deposits = DepositStress(withdrawal=0.25, withdrawal_date=datetime.date(2023, 3, 9))
end = datetime.date(2023, 3, 10)

hold = run(svb, Historical(), end=end, deposit_stress=run_on_deposits)
sell = run(svb, Historical(), end=end, deposit_stress=run_on_deposits, sell_afs_on=datetime.date(2023, 3, 8))

RunResult.statements holds the balance sheet and income statement for every market day, one row per line (date, section, account, balance). A small helper reads one line, in billions:

def line(result, day, account):
    s = result.statements
    row = s[(s["date"] == day) & (s["account"] == account)]
    return float(row["balance"].iloc[0]) / 1e6   # the Call Report is in USD thousands

for name, result in (("hold", hold), ("sell AFS", sell)):
    for day in (datetime.date(2023, 3, 7), datetime.date(2023, 3, 8), datetime.date(2023, 3, 9)):
        print(name, day,
              round(line(result, day, "Cash and Cash Equivalents"), 1),
              round(line(result, day, "Accumulated OCI"), 1),
              round(line(result, day, "net_income"), 1))
    print(name, "CET1", f"{result.metrics['CET1_RATIO'].dropna().iloc[-1]:.1%}")

docs.title: The results
docs.text:
USD billions; net income is for 2023 so far:

Run Day Cash Accumulated OCI Net income hold 7 Mar 15.5 −2.7 0.4 hold 9 Mar −28.4 −2.6 0.4 sell AFS 8 Mar 41.1 0.0 −2.2 sell AFS 9 Mar −2.7 0.0 −2.2

CET1 ratio on 10 March: 17.7% holding, 15.9% after the sale.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
• Selling turns an unrealised loss into a realised one. Before the sale, the AFS loss sat in accumulated OCI (−$2.7bn), outside profit and, with the AOCI filter, outside CET1. Selling moves it into the income statement (Investment Income (FVOCI) −$2.7bn), and net income for the year turns negative. Total equity hardly moves: the loss was already in equity, in AOCI. The regulatory ratio falls, because realised losses do count in CET1. SVB itself reported a $1.8bn loss on the $21bn it sold.
  • The cash was not enough. A quarter of deposits is $43.8bn. Holding everything, cash goes to −$28.4bn: a hole the bank must borrow to fill. Even after selling the whole AFS book, cash is −$2.7bn. The rest of the assets are loans and held-to-maturity securities, and the HTM securities were $14.1bn under water by then (hold.summary["unrealised_end"]["htm"]). Selling them would have realised that loss, almost all of the bank's equity.
  • Negative cash is the lab's signal of a funding gap. The lab does not borrow for you; it shows how much the bank would have had to raise.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• A slow run instead of a sudden one. Use Deposit run-off (% a year) (Python: DepositStress(runoff_rate=0.5)): the balance leaves continuously from the start date.
  • Different behaviour per deposit. Liquidity stress applies to every deposit. To give each its own, write a bank file: each deposit takes runoff_rate and withdrawals ([["2023-03-09", 0.25]]). Mark borrowings with "borrowing": true so a deposit stress leaves them alone. See the bank file reference and a bank from its Call Report, which shows how to get SVB's bank file to edit.
  • On the command line: python -m brms.lab run svb.zip --scenario historical --months 3 --withdrawal 0.25 --withdrawal-date 2023-03-09 --sell-afs-on 2023-03-08.

docs.title: brms
docs.text:
BRMS - Bank Risk Management Simulation.

BRMS is an educational tool designed to provide users with an in-depth understanding of bank risk management practices. It allows users to simulate and respond to various risk scenarios, and analyze the impact on a bank's financial health.

BRMS generally follows the Model-View-Controller (MVC) design pattern for maintainability. Additional modules are to implement core functionalities that are independent of the GUI.

Modules:

  • app –

    Application layer for BRMS: controllers and views.

  • core –

    Core domain logic for the BRMS bank simulation.

  • data –

    Default simulations: the scripts that build them and the zips they write.

  • lab –

    The stress-test lab: run a bank through rate scenarios and compare the results.

  • main –

    Main module for the BRMS application.

  • web –

    The stress-test lab in a browser: a FastAPI server over :mod:brms.lab and a static front end.

docs.title: profitability
docs.text:
Profitability over a trailing year, annualised: ROA, ROE, NIM, and interest-earning assets.

The window is the 365 days ending on the metric date, clipped to the first day with an ordinary (NORMAL) journal entry; flows are the windowed income statement scaled by 365 / days in window. With fewer than 30 days of history the metrics are undefined (None). Denominators are averages of the day's recorded metrics over the window's market days, so TOTAL_ASSETS, TOTAL_EQUITY and INTEREST_EARNING_ASSETS must be computed before these metrics.

  • InterestEarningAssetsMetric –

    Carrying value of open long bond and loan positions.

  • NetInterestMarginMetric –

    Net interest margin: annualised (interest income - interest expense) / average interest-earning assets.

  • ROAMetric –

    Return on assets: annualised net income / average total assets.

  • ROEMetric –

    Return on equity: annualised net income / average total equity.

docs.title: regulatory
docs.text:
Regulatory capital, RWA, capital ratios and the leverage ratio.

All figures for a day come from one :class:CapitalCalculator pass over the as-if-closed balance sheet and the day's valuations, shared by every metric in this module.

  • CET1 = total equity - (accumulated OCI if the AOCI filter is on) - intangible assets - preferred stock in equity.
  • Tier 1 = CET1 + preferred stock in equity + other AT1; Total capital = Tier 1 + Tier 2 (inputs).
  • Total RWA = credit RWA (standardised approach) + operational RWA (an input).
  • Leverage exposure = total assets - intangible assets (on-balance-sheet only).

Classes:

  • CET1CapitalMetric –

    Common Equity Tier 1 capital.

  • CET1RatioMetric –

    CET1 capital / total RWA (None when there is no RWA).

  • CapitalCalculator –

    Computes :class:CapitalFigures, memoised per (ledger, date, journal length, regulatory inputs).

  • CapitalFigures –

    The day's regulatory capital and risk figures.

  • CreditRWAMetric –

    Credit RWA, standardised approach.

  • LeverageRatioMetric –

    Tier 1 capital / leverage exposure measure.

  • OperationalRWAMetric –

    Operational RWA (an input).

  • Tier1CapitalMetric –

    Tier 1 capital.

  • Tier1RatioMetric –

    Tier 1 capital / total RWA.

  • TotalCapitalMetric –

    Total capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2).

  • TotalCapitalRatioMetric –

  • TotalRWAMetric –

docs.title: exposures
docs.text:
Credit RWA under the Basel standardised approach (CRE20), from per-position exposures.

Each open LONG bond or loan position is an exposure equal to its carrying value plus accrued interest on the day. The position is classified by its issuer and instrument type and weighted with the CRE20 tables in standardised_approach. Balance-sheet assets that are not positions (cash, property, interbank receivables) are weighted by account. An exposure that cannot be classified raises UnsupportedPositionError; nothing is weighted by default.

Classes:

  • CreditRWA –

    Credit RWA with its line items.

  • ExposureClass –

    Standardised-approach exposure classes the lab supports.

  • RWALine –

    One weighted exposure: a position (key = position id) or a balance-sheet account (key = name).

  • credit_rwa –

docs.title: assign_bucket
docs.text:
assign_bucket(remaining_years: float) -> int

Return the index of the IRRBB bucket for the given remaining years to repricing.

Buckets use half-open intervals (lower, upper] so that boundary values such as exactly 8.0 years fall into the 7Y-8Y bucket rather than 8Y-9Y. The overnight bucket (index 0) is a special case: it captures zero and any value up to and including its upper bound (i.e. [0, upper]).

Negative or zero values are assigned to the overnight bucket (index 0).

docs.title: eve
docs.text:
Economic value of equity under the Basel standardised interest-rate shocks (SRP31).

Each open long bond or loan position is revalued by discounting its remaining cash flows on the day's curve shifted by the scenario's zero-rate shock. Deposits with a core share (SRP31 stable non-maturity deposits) contribute the discounted run-off of their core balance; the rest reprices overnight. Mortgage-backed securities re-project their cash flows on each shocked curve, so prepayments speed up as rates fall (negative convexity). Floating-rate coupons are forecast from the engine's shared forwarding handle, which is relinked to the shocked curve for the scenario and restored afterwards. Only banking-book positions count (SRP31). Cash, deposits and interest payable count at book value: deposits are treated as repricing overnight, so they carry no duration, which makes rising-rate scenarios look worse than a behavioural deposit model would.

docs.title: AccountNormalBalance
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

The normal balance of an account or the preferred type of net balance that it should have.

In double-entry bookkeeping, every account has a "normal" side:

  • DEBIT_NORMAL: Asset and Expense accounts normally carry debit balances. Debits increase these accounts; credits decrease them.
  • CREDIT_NORMAL: Liability, Equity, and Income accounts normally carry credit balances. Credits increase these accounts; debits decrease them.

docs.title: AccountType
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

Types of accounts in the accounting equation.

The five fundamental account types:

  • Asset -- resources owned (debit-normal)
  • Liability -- obligations owed (credit-normal)
  • Equity -- residual interest (credit-normal)
  • Income -- revenue earned (credit-normal, temporary)
  • Expense -- costs incurred (debit-normal, temporary)

Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
