A chart of accounts organizes all accounts by category.

::

+----------------------------------------------+
|              Chart of Accounts                |
+----------------------------------------------+
| Assets        | What the entity owns          |
| Liabilities   | What the entity owes          |
| Equity        | Owner's residual interest     |
| Income        | Revenue earned (temporary)    |
| Expenses      | Costs incurred (temporary)    |
+----------------------------------------------+
| Accounting equation:                          |
|   Assets = Liabilities + Equity               |
|                                               |
| At period end, Income and Expenses close to   |
| Retained Earnings (Equity) via Income Summary |
+----------------------------------------------+

Composite T-account that can hold multiple sub T-accounts.

A composite account aggregates the balances of its children. Debiting or crediting a child automatically recalculates the parent's totals.

Example -- Investment Securities (composite)::

docs.title: TAccount
docs.text:
TAccount(
    name: str,
    account_type: AccountType,
    contra_accounts: list[TAccount] | None = None,
    parent: TAccount | None = None,
    debit: float = 0.0,
    credit: float = 0.0,
    description: str = "",
    *,
    is_contra_account: bool = False,
    is_temporary_account: bool = False,
)

A T-account in double-entry bookkeeping.

A T-account has two sides: debit (left) and credit (right). The normal balance determines which side increases the account value.

Asset and Expense accounts have DEBIT normal balance::

+----------------------------------+
|         Cash (Asset)             |
+-----------------+----------------+
|     Debit       |    Credit      |
|   (increase)    |   (decrease)   |
+-----------------+----------------+
|    1,000        |      200       |
|      500        |                |
+-----------------+----------------+
|   Balance: 1,300                 |
+----------------------------------+

Liability, Equity, and Income accounts have CREDIT normal balance::

+----------------------------------+
|       Deposits (Liability)       |
+-----------------+----------------+
|     Debit       |    Credit      |
|   (decrease)    |   (increase)   |
+-----------------+----------------+
|                 |    5,000       |
|      200        |    1,000       |
+-----------------+----------------+
|              Balance: 5,800      |
+----------------------------------+

Double-entry principle: every transaction debits one account and credits another for the same amount, keeping the books balanced.

Example: Receiving a $10,000 deposit::

Cash.debit(10_000)      -- Cash increases
Deposits.credit(10_000) -- Deposits increases

docs.title: AccountNormalBalance
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

The normal balance of an account or the preferred type of net balance that it should have.

In double-entry bookkeeping, every account has a "normal" side:

  • DEBIT_NORMAL: Asset and Expense accounts normally carry debit balances. Debits increase these accounts; credits decrease them.
  • CREDIT_NORMAL: Liability, Equity, and Income accounts normally carry credit balances. Credits increase these accounts; debits decrease them.

docs.title: AccountType
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

Types of accounts in the accounting equation.

The five fundamental account types:

  • Asset -- resources owned (debit-normal)
  • Liability -- obligations owed (credit-normal)
  • Equity -- residual interest (credit-normal)
  • Income -- revenue earned (credit-normal, temporary)
  • Expense -- costs incurred (debit-normal, temporary)

Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity

|      200        |    1,000       |
+-----------------+----------------+

Deposits.credit(10_000) -- Deposits increases

BankChartOfAccounts()

Bases: ChartOfAccounts

Pre-configured chart of accounts for a commercial bank.

Every account is accessible as a named attribute. Composite accounts automatically aggregate their sub-accounts. Contra accounts reduce the balance of the account they are attached to.

Account hierarchy::

Assets
├── Cash and Cash Equivalents
├── Receivables from Financial Institutions
├── Loans and Advances
│   └── Loan Loss Provision                ← contra
├── Assets at FVTPL (Trading Book)
├── Investment Securities                  ← composite
│   ├── Investment Securities at Amortized Cost (HTM)
│   └── Investment Securities at FVOCI
├── Property, Plant and Equipment
└── Intangible Assets

Liabilities
├── Deposits and Other Public Borrowings   ← composite
│   ├── Deposits (Customer)
│   └── Other Public Borrowings
├── Payables to Financial Institutions
└── Debt Issues

Equity
├── Shareholders' Equity
└── Accumulated OCI                        ← composite
    ├── Unrealized OCI Gain
    └── Unrealized OCI Loss                ← contra

Income
├── Interest Income                        ← composite
├── Trading Income (FVTPL)                 ← composite
│   ├── Unrealized Trading Gain
│   ├── Realized Trading Gain
│   ├── Unrealized Trading Loss
│   └── Realized Trading Loss
└── Investment Income (FVOCI)              ← composite
    ├── Realized OCI Gain
    └── Realized OCI Loss

Expenses
├── Interest Expense
├── Operating Expense
└── Income Tax Expense

|              Chart of Accounts                |

docs.title: ledger
docs.text:
General ledger: posts journal entries to accounts and closes the books at period end.

The ledger is the core of the double-entry bookkeeping system. It holds a :class:ChartOfAccounts (the accounts) and a :class:Journal (the record of all entries). Posting an entry simultaneously records it in the journal and updates the affected T-account balances.

Posting flow::

JournalEntry ──> Ledger.post()
                   ├── journal.add_entry(entry)    (audit trail)
                   ├── account.debit(amount)       (for each debit leg)
                   └── account.credit(amount)      (for each credit leg)

Period-end closing sequence::

1. close_contra_accounts()
   Contra income/expense balances are netted against their parent accounts.

2. close_income_and_expense_accounts()
   All income and expense account balances transfer to Income Summary.

3. close_income_summary_account()
   Income Summary balance transfers to Retained Earnings.

docs.title: mbs
docs.text:
Agency mortgage pass-through securities with a rate-dependent prepayment model.

A pass-through pays its holders, each month, interest at the pass-through coupon_rate on the pool balance plus all principal the borrowers repay: the scheduled principal of a level-payment mortgage at the pool's note rate (wac), re-amortised every month over the remaining term, and prepayments. Prepayments are a share SMM = 1 - (1 - CPR)^(1/12) of the balance left after scheduled principal.

Two speeds are used (a deliberate simplification):

  • Realised paydowns follow a constant pricing_cpr fixed when the pool is set up. The security is a QuantLib amortising fixed-rate bond with those notionals, so interest accrual, settlement, principal paydowns and the ledger work exactly as for amortising loans.
  • Valuation re-projects the remaining cash flows from the current balance at the CPR the :class:PrepaymentModel gives for today's curve (:meth:MortgageBackedSecurity.projected_leg). Rising rates slow prepayments and lengthen the pool (extension); falling rates speed them up and cap price gains (negative convexity). Fair value, spread calibration and EVE use it.

So realised cash flows do not respond to rates; only values do.

Classes:

  • MortgageBackedSecurity –

    An agency mortgage pass-through security (monthly, 30/360, no payment delay).

  • PrepaymentModel –

    Annual prepayment speed (CPR) as an S-curve in the refinancing incentive.

    mortgage_spread: float = 0.017,

Annual prepayment speed (CPR) as an S-curve in the refinancing incentive.

incentive = wac - mortgage rate, with the mortgage rate taken as the curve's 10-year zero rate (semi-annual) plus mortgage_spread. The CPR rises from turnover_cpr (housing turnover, no refinancing) to max_cpr, reaching the midpoint at refi_center; refi_width sets how quickly.

docs.title: interest_accrual
docs.text:
InterestIncomeAccrualRule: accrues interest income using QuantLib conventions.

For QL-backed bonds, uses bond.accruedAmount(date) which correctly handles day count conventions (e.g., Thirty360), business day adjustments, and coupon period boundaries. The accrual is the change in QL's accrued interest between the previous simulation date and today.

Any difference between the sum of daily accruals and the coupon payment amount is handled as a "catch-up" at settlement by the CouponPaymentRule.

Instruments without a QuantLib object are not supported and raise.

docs.title: scaled_accrued_amount
docs.text:
scaled_accrued_amount(
    ql_inst: Bond, ql_date: Date
) -> Decimal

Return the absolute accrued interest at ql_date in currency.

QL's accruedAmount(d) returns per-100 of the current notional at d. For fixed-notional bonds the current notional equals face value; for amortizing instruments it declines at each payment date. In both cases, scaling by notional(d) / 100 gives the correct dollar amount.

docs.title: loan_interest_settlement
docs.text:
LoanInterestSettlementRule: settles interest on amortizing loan payment dates.

On each scheduled interest payment date, the borrower remits the interest portion of the monthly payment. The accounting entry clears the Accrued Interest Receivable built up by daily InterestIncomeAccrualRule postings:

Dr  Cash                         (scheduled interest amount)
Cr  Accrued Interest Receivable  (what was actually accrued)
Cr  Interest Income              (catch-up difference)

This follows the same three-leg settlement pattern as CouponPaymentRule for bonds — the AccountingService handles the metadata identically.

MarkToMarketRule: moves an FVOCI or FVTPL position's carrying value to its clean fair value.

The amount is FAIR_VALUE(today) - CARRYING_VALUE(previous record) - change in AMORTIZED_COST today. The last term is zero for FVTPL; for FVOCI it has already been booked to interest income by the EffectiveInterestRule, so the mark carries only the change in unrealised gain or loss.

docs.title: AmortizedCostCalculator
docs.text:
AmortizedCostCalculator()

Computes acquisition-related values and amortised cost of a position.

Bonds are amortised at the effective interest rate: the yield, compounded at the bond's coupon frequency on its own day counter, that prices the remaining cash flows at the position's clean cost on the acquisition date. Amortised cost on a date is the clean price at that yield, so amortised cost plus accrued interest is the present value of the remaining cash flows at the effective rate.

Keeps the QL PrimeIndex fixing history in sync with MarketDataStore.

The MarketDataStore is authoritative. This service projects the 'benchmarks' frame into QL's global IndexManager, one-way and incrementally.

docs.text:
OperatingService: the day's operating expense, fee income and income tax for the whole bank.

These flows belong to no position. They are booked after the day's position transactions, so the tax accrual sees the day's profit: tax to date = rate x max(0, pre-tax profit of the period), and the day's tax is the change in that amount (a reversal when profit falls).

docs.title: reinvestment
docs.text:
Reinvest maturing bonds: replace each with a new par bond of the same term at the day's rate.

Used when Bank.reinvest_maturities is set (the static-balance-sheet assumption of supervisory stress tests). The new bond has the matured bond's face, term (in months), issuer, rating, measurement basis, book and credit spread; its coupon is the par rate on the day's curve plus that spread, so it is bought at face with no accrued interest. Loans are not rolled over.

docs.text:
ReportingService — pure computation of financial statements from a Ledger.

The balance sheet is produced "as if closed" on the reporting date: a deep copy of the ledger is closed so that income and expenses are transferred to Retained Earnings. The original ledger is never modified.

ReportingService()

Generate structured financial statement data from a Ledger.

All methods are pure computations — no HTML, no UI concerns. The as-if-closed balance sheet is memoised per (ledger, date, journal length) on the instance, so every metric on a day shares one deep copy of the ledger; the journal only grows, so a new posting changes the key.

docs.title: rule_engine
docs.text:
Position-aware RuleEngine: applies accounting rules to open positions.

Rules are executed in a defined priority order to ensure logical consistency:

  1. Accruals — recognize earned/owed amounts (no cash movement)
  2. Mark-to-market — revalue positions to fair value
  3. Cash flows — coupon payments, interest settlements, amortization
  4. Maturity — settle and close positions (must be last)

docs.title: advance
docs.text:
advance(date: date | None = None) -> None

Advance the simulation by one calendar day (or to an explicit date).

Steps performed (in order): 1. Determine the target date (next calendar day or explicit). 2. Fetch market state if available for this date. 3. Value all positions (every day; the curve is rebuilt on market-data days). 4. Apply rules via the rule engine to obtain transactions. 5. Post all transactions to the ledger via the accounting service. 6. Record the transaction batch in the transaction log. 7. Compute metrics (only on market-data days). 8. Emit granular events and :class:DateAdvanced.

An explicit date more than one day after the current date processes every intervening calendar day in order, so no accrual, coupon or amortisation is skipped.

Set the simulation state after loading a snapshot with opening balances.

The snapshot represents ledger state as of start_date - 1. Setting _current_date to that date ensures the first advance() sees a proper previous_date — accrual rules then compute the correct one-day delta instead of reposting from the last coupon/payment reset.

docs.title: spreads
docs.text:
Per-position credit spreads over the discount curve.

A spread is a constant continuously compounded zero-rate spread (a decimal, 0.01 = 100bp) added to the day's curve when valuing one position. Calibrating it on the acquisition (or as-of) date to the price actually paid isolates rate risk: from then on, fair value moves only with the curve, and non-Treasury bonds and loans no longer jump on their first mark.

docs.title: valuation_strategies
docs.text:
Valuation strategies: record the per-position values the ledger is reconciled against.

For every open bond or loan position, on every calendar day from its acquisition date:

  • ACCRUED_INTEREST — coupon interest earned since the last coupon date (currency).
  • AMORTIZED_COST — clean acquisition cost rolled forward at the effective interest rate (bonds) or clean cost less scheduled principal (loans). Not recorded for FVTPL positions.
  • FAIR_VALUE — clean fair value: NPV on the day's curve less accrued interest. Bonds only, on market-data days and on and after the maturity date (where it is face value).
  • CARRYING_VALUE — what the investment or loan account holds for the position.

Classes:

  • CarryingValueStrategy –

    Amortised-cost positions: carrying value is amortised cost; bonds also get a fair value.

  • DepositStrategy –

    Deposits: the balance (CARRYING_VALUE) and interest payable (ACCRUED_INTEREST).

  • FairValueStrategy –

    FVOCI and FVTPL positions: carrying value follows clean fair value.

  • ValuationStrategy –

DepositStrategy()

The balance is the acquired balance times the deposit's run-off and withdrawal factor. The day's interest is balance x rate / 365, where the rate moves from its acquisition value by beta times the change in the reference yield, floored at zero. docs.title: data
docs.text:
Default simulations: the scripts that build them and the zips they write.

The scripts read raw market data from DEFAULT_DATA_FOLDER (market/ beside this file, versioned): treasury_yields.csv and, for the Prime-linked banks, prime_rates.csv. Each writes its zip next to itself with :func:brms.core.services.snapshot_writer.save_snapshot; python -m brms.data.build_all writes all of them. The zips are gitignored build artifacts that every distribution build requires (see hatch_build.py).

Modules:

  • build_all –

    Build every default simulation zip from the versioned market data: python -m brms.data.build_all.

  • create_case_studies –

    Build the case-study banks from the Call Reports saved in call_reports/ (public FDIC data).

  • create_ci_loan_prime –

    Generate ci_loan_prime.zip -- Prime-indexed variable-rate C&I loan.

  • create_diversified_bank –

    Generate diversified_bank.zip -- 2-3 instruments per major type.

  • create_fvtpl_bond –

    Generate fvtpl_bond.zip -- a single FVTPL Corporate Bond.

  • create_htm_treasury –

    Generate htm_treasury.zip -- a single HTM Treasury Note.

  • create_mortgage –

    Generate mortgage.zip -- a single 30Y Residential Mortgage.

docs.title: create_ci_loan_prime
docs.text:
Generate ci_loan_prime.zip -- Prime-indexed variable-rate C&I loan.

Simulation start date: 2022-01-04.

Instrument              Basis            Amount     Acquired     Side   Book
--------------------    ---------------  ---------  ----------   -----  -------
Common Equity           NA               2,000,000  2021-06-01   SHORT  BANKING
Term Deposit 2%         NA               3,000,000  2021-06-01   SHORT  BANKING
Prime+250bp 5Y CI Loan  AMORTIZED_COST   5,000,000  2021-06-01   LONG   BANKING

The C&I loan is a bullet (no amortization) variable-rate loan indexed to U.S. Bank Prime Rate plus 250 basis points, repricing monthly. The simulation window catches the 2022 Fed tightening cycle where Prime rose from 3.25% to 7.50%.

Run::

uv run python src/brms/data/create_ci_loan_prime.py

Yields are extracted from the existing htm_treasury.zip. Market data is read from treasury_yields.csv and prime_rates.csv in the data folder (default src/brms/data/market).

    Write the CI loan simulation zip to out_path and return its path.

docs.text:
Generate diversified_bank.zip -- 2-3 instruments per major type.

Simulation start date: 2022-01-04.

Instrument                  Basis            Amount     Acquired     Side   Book
========================    ===============  =========  ==========   =====  =======
Common Equity               NA               2,000,000  2021-01-04   SHORT  BANKING
Retained Earnings           NA                 500,000  2021-01-04   SHORT  BANKING
Demand Deposit (0%)         NA               3,000,000  2021-01-04   SHORT  BANKING
Savings Deposit (0.5%)      NA               4,000,000  2021-01-04   SHORT  BANKING
Term Deposit (2%)           NA               5,000,000  2021-01-04   SHORT  BANKING
10Y Treasury 3.5% HTM       AMORTIZED_COST    (NPV)    2021-01-04   LONG   BANKING
5Y Treasury 2.5% HTM        AMORTIZED_COST    (NPV)    2021-01-04   LONG   BANKING
5Y Corp Bond 4.5% FVOCI     FVOCI             (NPV)    2021-06-01   LONG   BANKING
3Y Corp Bond 3.5% FVTPL     FVTPL             (NPV)    2021-01-04   LONG   TRADING
7Y Corp Bond 5.0% FVTPL     FVTPL             (NPV)    2021-01-04   LONG   TRADING
30Y Res Mortgage 5%         AMORTIZED_COST  (outstand)  2021-01-04   LONG   BANKING
15Y Res Mortgage 4%         AMORTIZED_COST  (outstand)  2021-06-01   LONG   BANKING
Prime+250bp 5Y C&I Loan     AMORTIZED_COST   3,000,000  2021-06-01   LONG   BANKING
Prime+175bp 3Y Revolver     AMORTIZED_COST   2,000,000  2021-06-01   LONG   BANKING

Bond acquisition costs are QuantLib NPV at acquisition date. Mortgage/loan acquisition costs are QL outstanding balance at acquisition date.

Run::

uv run python src/brms/data/create_diversified_bank.py [data_folder]

Where data_folder contains treasury_yields.csv and prime_rates.csv. If omitted, src/brms/data/market is used.

docs.title: create_fvtpl_bond
docs.text:
Generate fvtpl_bond.zip -- a single FVTPL Corporate Bond.

Simulation start date: 2022-01-04.

Instrument              Basis            Amount     Acquired     Side   Book
────────────────────    ───────────────  ─────────  ──────────   ─────  ───────
Common Equity           NA               1,000,000  2021-01-04   SHORT  BANKING
Customer Deposit (0%)   NA               6,000,000  2021-06-01   SHORT  BANKING
5Y Corp Bond 4% FVTPL   FVTPL             (NPV)    2021-03-15   LONG   TRADING

Bond: issued 2020-06-01, 5Y, 4% semi-annual coupon, matures 2025-06-01. Deposit carries 0% interest. Bond acquisition cost is QuantLib NPV at acquisition date. The bond is classified as Fair Value Through Profit or Loss (FVTPL) in the trading book — mark-to-market gains and losses flow directly through the income statement.

Run::

uv run python src/brms/data/create_fvtpl_bond.py <data_folder>

docs.title: bank_file
docs.text:
Build a simulation from a point-in-time bank file: positions as of one date, no acquisition history.

bank.json::

{
  "name": "...", "as_of": "2021-12-31",
  "regulatory": {"aoci_filter": false, "operational_rwa": "...", ...},   # optional
  "operating": {"noninterest_expense": 2.2e9, "noninterest_income": 8e8, "tax_rate": 0.21},  # optional, per year
  "cash": 1000000,
  "other_assets": 50000, "other_liabilities": 20000,   # optional: carried unchanged, not modelled
  "intangible_assets": 10000,                           # optional: goodwill etc., deducted from CET1
  "deposits": [{"id": "dep", "name": "Savings", "balance": 2500000, "interest_rate": 0.001,
                "beta": 0.3, "runoff_rate": 0.05, "withdrawals": [["2022-03-09", 0.25]]}],   # optional
  "positions": [
    {"id": "ust", "type": "treasury_note", <instrument terms>, "issuer": {...},
     "basis": "AMORTIZED_COST" | "FVOCI" | "FVTPL", "book": "BANKING" | "TRADING",
     "amortized_cost": 980000, "fair_value": 950000}
  ]
}

Values are clean (excluding accrued interest). amortized_cost is required at amortised cost and FVOCI; fair_value is required at FVOCI and FVTPL and optional at amortised cost. Each position is treated as bought at close of business on the as-of date at its amortised cost (its fair value for FVTPL), so its effective interest rate is solved from the book value; its credit spread is calibrated to the reported fair value, or to the book value if none is given. Equity is the balancing figure. An FVOCI position's reported unrealised gain or loss enters accumulated OCI with the first day's mark.

docs.title: call_report
docs.text:
Build a bank file from a US bank's Call Report (via the FDIC BankFind financials API).

The Call Report (FFIEC 031/041) gives a bank's balance sheet each quarter, including how its debt securities and loans spread over remaining-maturity (or next-repricing) buckets. Those buckets are enough to give the lab a bank with the right interest-rate profile:

  • Securities (Schedule RC-B, Memorandum 2: HTM at amortised cost plus AFS at fair value). Non-mortgage debt per maturity bucket becomes a bullet bond at the bucket midpoint, split between Treasuries (sovereign) and other issuers (agency/municipal, treated as PSEs). Mortgage pass-throughs per remaining-maturity bucket become agency MBS pools with that remaining term. Other MBS (CMOs, CMBS) per expected-average-life bucket become bullets at 2 and 6 years. Each class splits between HTM and AFS in the bank's overall proportions, or as given by afs (the data does not say which securities are in which book), so the HTM and AFS totals, and their fair values, match the report. All securities carry the bank's securities yield.
  • Loans (Schedule RC-C, Memorandum 2) by remaining maturity or next repricing, scaled to net loans. Loans repricing within 3 months are Prime floaters; the rest are amortising fixed-rate loans (1-4 family loans as residential mortgages) at the bucket midpoint, at the loan yield.
  • Funding: noninterest-bearing deposits; interest-bearing deposits at the bank's deposit cost, repricing with deposit_beta of the 3-month yield; other borrowings, fed funds purchased and subordinated debt as one floating-rate liability.
  • Operating flows: non-interest expense and income, annualised, and the effective tax rate.
  • Operational-risk RWA estimated with the Basel III standardised approach from a simplified business indicator (loss multiplier 1), so capital ratios are not on credit RWA alone.
  • Equity is the balancing figure (bank_file); items not modelled (trading assets, premises, intangibles, other assets and liabilities) explain its gap to reported equity, which is kept under "reported" with the reported capital figures.

Values stay in USD thousands, as reported. Income items are year-to-date and are annualised. Interest-bearing deposits pass through deposit_beta (default 0.35) of moves in the 3-month Treasury yield; noninterest-bearing deposits pay nothing; no deposit runs off unless you say so.

    Return a bank file (see :mod:brms.lab.bank_file) built from Call Report items.

    Return operational-risk RWA from a simplified business indicator (BI), in the inputs' units.

    noninterest_income: float,
    unit: float = 1.0,

Return operational-risk RWA from a simplified business indicator (BI), in the inputs' units.

docs.title: svb
docs.text:
Acceptance case: Silicon Valley Bank through the 2022 rate rise.

SVB Financial Group's balance sheet at 31 December 2021 (Form 10-K FY2021, USD millions) is rebuilt as a point-in-time bank file and run through actual 2022 Treasury yields. The engine's unrealised losses on held-to-maturity (HTM) and available-for-sale (AFS) securities at the end of 2022 are compared, as a share of amortised cost, with those SVB reported at 31 December 2022 (Form 10-K FY2022):

======== =============== ========== ================= Book Amortised cost Fair value Unrealised (rate) ======== =============== ========== ================= HTM 2021 98,202 97,227 -975 (-1.0%) HTM 2022 91,327 76,169 -15,158 (-16.6%) AFS 2021 27,370 27,221 -149 (-0.5%) AFS 2022 28,602 26,069 -2,533 (-8.9%) ======== =============== ========== =================

Three cases. In the first two, each book is one fixed-rate bullet bond with the portfolio's reported weighted-average yield as coupon and a maturity chosen so that its modified duration at that yield equals a target: the durations SVB reported at the start (HTM 4.1 years, AFS 3.5) and at the end (6.2 and 3.6, after the extension that actually happened). A bullet bond cannot extend. In the third, the HTM book, mostly agency MBS, is one pass-through pool (coupon = book yield, note rate 50bp higher, 25 years remaining, default prepayment model), whose projected prepayments slow as rates rise. SVB's 2022 trading (AFS sales and purchases, the removal of AFS hedges) is not replayed, so rates are compared, not amounts.

Run python -m brms.lab.examples.svb for the comparison table.

docs.title: svb_call_report
docs.text:
SVB from its own Call Report: the bank (Silicon Valley Bank, FDIC certificate 24735) at 31 Dec 2021.

Unlike :mod:brms.lab.examples.svb, which rebuilds the holding company's 10-K balance sheet by hand, this case uses only the bank's Call Report as the FDIC publishes it (saved alongside this module as svb_call_report_20211231.json, so it runs offline) through :mod:brms.lab.call_report. The bank is run through actual 2022 yields and its unrealised losses, as a share of amortised cost, are compared with its Call Report at 31 Dec 2022:

====== =============== ========== =========== Book Amortised cost Fair value Unrealised ====== =============== ========== =========== HTM 91,327,000 76,168,000 -16.6% AFS 28,502,000 25,976,000 -8.9% ====== =============== ========== ===========

(USD thousands.) Two cases: the Call Report alone, where every security class splits between HTM and AFS in the bank's overall proportion, and the same with the AFS mix from SVB Financial's 10-K (mostly Treasuries), since the Call Report data used does not say which securities are in which book. Run python -m brms.lab.examples.svb_call_report.

docs.title: JobManager
docs.text:
JobManager(factory: Callable[[], Executor])

Runs jobs in worker processes, one process per job, and records the outcome.

A worker that dies abruptly (killed for memory, a crash in native code) breaks a process pool for good; the next submission replaces the pool with a fresh one from factory.

    Cancel queued jobs, stop running ones, and wait until the workers have gone.

docs.title: jobs
docs.text:
Work done in worker processes: building banks, summarising them and running scenarios.

Every function here is module-level (picklable), takes plain data and writes its output to disk, so the server never imports QuantLib state into its own process. The engine is imported inside the functions: the server imports this module at start, and on a fresh install the first import of pandas or QuantLib takes many seconds.

  • ignore_interrupts –

docs.title: workspace
docs.text:
On-disk workspace of the web app: banks, runs and their results.

::

<data dir>/
  banks/<id>/  bank.zip, bank.json (if built from a bank file), meta.json, summary.json
  runs/<id>/   meta.json, payload.json, result.pkl
  cache/       summaries of the packaged demo banks

The server process only reads and writes these files; engine work happens in worker processes.
